subtopic: STATEMENTS OF DR. ENDICOTT  DECISION CONCERNING LEGAL ACTION

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENTS OF DR. ENDICOTT  DECISION CONCERNING LEGAL ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at previous sittings of the house two members of the opposition have raised the question as to what action was to be taken with regard to Dr. James G. Endicott. I should like now to make a brief statement on the subject.
The Department of Justice has examined two issues of a communist publication entitled "Peace Review" and Dr. James G. Endicott's speech at Winnipeg of June 18, 1952, in order to determine whether Dr. Endicott and the publishers of this pamphlet should be prosecuted.
There is little in this speech of June 18 or these pamphlets which was not already contained in a speech of Dr. Endicott at Maple Leaf Gardens on May 11 last.
Dr. Endicott, as is well known, is an ordained minister of the gospel and a Doctor of Divinity. He is obviously permitting himself to be used as a tool by which the propaganda of the atheistic communist party is spread throughout the world, and I do not think that very many Canadians will be taken in by his statements. According to the information available to the Department of Justice, the activities of such people as Dr. Endicott and the promoters of the Canadian peace congress have had very little effect on public opinion.
It is probable that the ringleaders of the communist conspiracy would like us to prosecute their dupes and tools such as Dr. Endicott and the publishers and distributors of these peace pamphlets. Prosecution would give them more publicity and might give them the appearance of martyrs. It would probably not embarrass the communists if Dr. Endicott were prosecuted and convicted. On the contrary, it is altogether likely that their interests would be served by a conviction. So far as Dr. Endicott himself is concerned, a prosecution and conviction could add little to the discredit he has already brought upon himself by allying himself with the forces of oppression, terror and atheism. It is felt that the advantages of conducting a prosecution against him would be more than offset by the disadvantages.
The freedom of speech which Dr. Endicott has been so consistently abusing is the freedom of speech which all Canadian citizens enjoy. The freedom of the press which the Canadian peace congress abuses is the freedom of the press which every newspaper in Canada uses from day to day to discuss public events and criticize or defend government policy. These freedoms are what we regard as the fundamental rights of every citizen and of the press in a free society under democratic government. They are indivisible. In our consideration of Dr. Endicott's obvious abuse of these freedoms, we must be careful not to do anything to injure or destroy the freedom of all Canadian citizens and of all Canadian newspapers.
For these and other reasons, following the example of other free countries like the United Kingdom and France, the government of Canada proposes to take no action at this time against Dr. Endicott for his public support of the communist party line in the allegations, such as the libellous and false assertion that the United States, operating as part of the United Nations forces in Korea, is waging germ warfare. '
Each of Dr. Endicott's statements and each act of publication and of distribution of these pamphlets is a separate episode in the operation of the tools of the communist party in Canada. The fact that the government does not think that it is upon balance wise to prosecute for these acts now does not mean, of course, that Dr. Endicott and the publishers are being absolved from responsibility for their acts. Each of these acts has been noted

Questions
and if the time should come when it seemed wise to prosecute, each of them will be taken into account.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to preface my remarks by saying that there can be no disagreement with what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said with regard to freedom of speech, but is it not a fact that under the law as it now exists there would be no ground whatever for the prosecution of any person making statements such as Dr. Endicott has made, so long as they have to do with another country within the United Nations? speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RETIRING ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members will find in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday the report made by the standing committee on banking and commerce recommending legislation for the purpose of establishing a pension plan after long service for members of the House of Commons on the basis of contributions equal to the contributions required by the Civil Service Superannuation Act and to be matched by like contributions from the treasury as is the case under the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Hon. members will recall that when I gave notice in the house of the motion to refer the subject matter of a pension plan for members to the standing committee on banking and commerce I stated that a number of hon. members had been working for a long time on the preparation of a plan which had been examined by the superintendent of insurance, his actuaries and by experts from the Department of Finance, and that the plan appeared to them to be actuarially sound. I pointed out that if it were felt generally in the house that the establishment of such a pension plan would strengthen our parliamentary institution by removing to a certain degree the feeling that long years spent in the public service made it impossible for a man to provide adequately for his later years such a plan would be of a nature to encourage the right kind of men to run for public office and afterwards, when they had acquired experience, to remain in public life as long as their constituents wished them to do so, it might be considered.
I said that if a sound scheme could be devised it would not be apt to meet with.

objections on the part of the government because I had made sure before making that statement in the house, by discussing the matter with the leader of the official opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Social Credit group, that they felt as I did that it was something that should be envisaged not merely in the interests of those who happened to be members of parliament at the present time. It was our view that if it was something that was merely going to be in their interest it should not be considered. However, if the opinion was that it was something that would really strengthen our parliamentary institution and make it easier to get and keep in parliament the kind of representatives necessary for the health of a democratic system, then, on the assurance that it was not going to be a partisan football of any kind and was something upon which there was general agreement by those who were more concerned about the interests of the public generally than the interests of their colleagues, for whom of course they have great friendship, I said that I would put the matter before my colleagues and get their authority to have the matter referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce. Before that committee the actuaries could be heard and could report what past experience would seem to indicate would happen under this kind of fund, and if it was felt to be the right thing by the committee there could be a recommendation [DOT] made as to the legislation required.
Of course I pointed out that any legislation would have to be preceded by a resolution and that such a resolution would have to be accompanied by the recommendation of the governor general as required by our constitution and by the standing orders of the house, but that if such were the development there would not be apt to be objections that could not be overcome so far as the constitutional requirements of the British North America Act and our standing orders are concerned. This resolution is the fulfilment of the implied undertaking I gave that if there was such a recommendation a resolution would be forthcoming. The purpose of the resolution is to enable the house to consider the legislation recommended by the standing committee on banking and commerce. I have gone over the bill. It is in print and I think it is already in the hands of hon. members.

speechtext:
It is ready to be put in the hands of hon. members as soon as the resolution is adopted, and the terms of the recommendation, with which the bill to be introduced conforms, are included in the
Members of Parliament-Pensions committee's report in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings. I have looked at them and they appear to be in line with the proposal that I had seen before the matter was referred to the committee, and about which I had ascertained from the superintendent of insurance and from the experts of the finance department that it was apt to be actuarially sound and a matter that would operate without any further charge on the public funds than the matching of the contributions to be made by all the members of parliament.
If that be so, and I have every reason to believe that it is so, it means that something of the order of $60,000 annually would be required to be placed in this fund and would suffice, with the contributions of the members, to provide for this additional security quite substantially although it will not operate in favour of very many of our members. It is the result of everyone being a collaborator in creating this security that makes it possible; but past experience has demonstrated that there will not be a substantial portion of the members of parliament in whose benefit it is apt to operate. That is like all co-operative undertakings. One does not know who will be in a situation where the benefits from the scheme would be very desirable but one does know that the additional feeling of security will be shared by all.
That being the case I feel it is a privilege, not as Prime Minister but as leader of the house, to provide all the necessary requirements to make it possible for the house to give consideration to this plan. If it comes to the conclusion to which it is apt to come from the information I have received I think it is a good thing and in the public interest to have it made law and become operative.
Once again, had I not had the assurance that the leaders of all parties of the house objectively felt that this was a good thing and in the public interest generally I would not have taken the responsibility of getting the authority of my colleagues to sponsor it. I know there is one hon. member who feels otherwise about it and perhaps there are others. So far one hon. member has expressed the view that there should not be in the case of members of parliament any contribution whatsoever from the public treasury to this pension fund. With that personally I do not agree. I do not see why those who serve their fellow citizens in parliament should not be entitled to the same consideration from their fellow citizens as the gentlemen who administer justice on the benches of our courts and as the officials who serve in the administration of our public affairs.
I have heard the suggestion that this would somehow lower the dignity of members of parliament. With that I am not in agreement.

Members of Parliament-Pensions 1 know, and all hon. members know, that the dignity of the Lord Chancellor of the United Kingdom has never been affected by the fact that on becoming Lord Chancellor he gets the assurance of an allowance to continue throughout the whole of his natural life. I do not think that the dignity of the present Prime Minister of the United Kingdom has in the least bit been affected by the fact that the legislation of the United Kingdom provides that a former prime minister is entitled to a pension from the public funds without, as I understand it, any contribution at all. Here is a contributory system which if it is set up shows the desire of each one of us to make his contribution, that will give a feeling of security to each and every one, although we all know there is probably not more than one in twenty who will ever be in a position where actual benefits to himself will materialize.
I am inclined to think that most of our people in Canada are reasonably minded and that they will feel that this is a laudable thing for members of parliament to do for each other, and that by doing it for each other they are performing a service to the public generally by strengthening our parliamentary institution.

As I was saying when I was interrupted, Mr. Chairman, the people of Canada should not have to contribute in order to provide pensions for members of parliament. The burden of taxation on our people is far too heavy now. It can only be described as crushing. Just to give one example, we have the 10 per cent sales tax, the highest rate there has ever been in the history of this nation. That tax is payable by everyone, poor and rich alike. Canadians should not now be called upon to help pay for security for members of parliament. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has put the matter in those words; he has said it would be a nice thing for members of parliament to have an additional feeling of security.
May I remind the committee that just today we shall be considering a vote of over $2 billion for defence purposes, in preparation to defend this country and to prevent a third world war which, if it comes, may well mean the wiping out of our nation. The taxpayers of Canada are having to provide over $2 billion in this very year for these defence purposes. I do not see how, under those circumstances, hon. members can justify calling upon the taxpayers to provide a further amount, no matter how small it is, in order to help members of parliament.
I would also point out that during this very week we considered the War Veterans Allowance Act which is a measure for the benefit of men who fought in the front line for this country. In my opinion the provisions made in that measure were entirely inadequate. In addition, these men are still subject to a means test. They have to pass a means test in order to get this miserably
Members of Parliament-Pensions small amount. There is no means test, however, in this pension scheme for members of parliament.
What will probably follow the enactment of a measure of this kind will be that most of the provincial legislatures will bring in similar measures. They will take the attitude that if members of parliament are entitled to a pension scheme, then so are the members of provincial legislatures. That is exactly what happened when the house raised the indemnity for members some years ago; it was not long until the various legislatures were doing the same thing. We set an example when we enact a measure of this kind.
I see no reason whatever for rushing through a measure of this kind in the dying days of the session. The details of the scheme have been available to the public only since the last week end. There has been no opportunity for people across the country to consider whether or not the scheme is a wise one. I think if a fair scheme could have been brought down there would have been general support for it across the country. But there has been no opportunity whatever for the press of Canada or the people of Canada to form an opinion on this particular scheme. We are asked to debate it today when we have not even the reports of what went on in this committee. There was quite an extended questioning carried on in the committee, and various other proposals were discussed. Government officials explained other plans. Yet we have not the reprint of those proceedings.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that this plan should stand over until the next session. That procedure would give time for thorough consideration not only by the members of the house but also by the people. Nobody is going to be hurt if the plan stands over. The pension would not be payable to anyone before the next election which we all understand is not to take place until after the next session. I repeat that no one would be hurt by letting this plan stand over until the next session. I believe that if that were done a better plan could be worked out. There is altogether too much haste, too much anxiety to get this through in a hurry; and we usually find that when that condition exists the measure as finally enacted does not turn out to be as sound as it would be in the ordinary case.	.

I have been studying this matter in my mind for many months. The general proposal has been known to me for at least four months and some of the details for six or eight months. That would apply to the members of all parties.
I wish to make it abundantly clear that I do not think this measure is being rushed through, nor do I wish the committee to take hasty action even now. I should like to see every member given the fullest opportunity to study it and to bring himself fully into knowledge of what we are doing.
I honour any member who feels that he cannot support this legislation, if he stands up and says so and gives his reason. He has that right. I do not hold it against the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra or the hon. member for Kamloops for taking the position they have. I have always found them to be men of great courage, men who were prepared to fight for their convictions, so I am not going to say one word now or at any other time against the stand they have taken. I have definite reasons for feeling that a scheme of this kind will strengthen our parliamentary institutions. I am not going to speak at length, and 1 have not asked my colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge, if I could use this illustration. The hon. member for Lethbridge came into this house in 1935 when he was requested by his people to stand for election. I do not know of any time in his life when he has sought to represent his people. He did not seek to represent them; he was sought by his people and asked to stand. He did stand and was elected at a time when he was at the height of his earning powers.
He has been in this house seventeen years during which time he has passed the most lucrative earning years of his life. Anyone who thinks that a member can stay in this House of Commons and do his duty toward the people of the country and accumulate anything honestly just does not know anything about it. He just cannot do it.
In addition my colleague surrendered seventeen years of pension rights in the professional body to which he belonged in the province of Alberta. He did that in order to serve the public and he can never get back those rights. He is at the point of years now where it would be impossible for him to start over again. Such surrender of rights is a serious thing for any man, I do not care who he is. The same thing can be said for the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who is in exactly the same position.
These are things which must be considered seriously. When anyone says that it does not strengthen our parliamentary institutions to have a measure of this kind, I do not think he has thought through the details. It is all right for a man who has a profession to which he can go back every week end and keep up his earning powers. That is true largely of the legal profession, but who wants this House of Commons to be made up of lawyers entirely? I think I speak for the general public when I say that we want some lawyers, but we do not want all members to be lawyers.
Then there are hon. members who belong to other professions which they can carry on and keep up their earning capacity over the years. By and large, if we are to have a parliamentary representation that is a crosssection of the people we must have some arrangement of this kind. Otherwise we are going to eliminate the possibility of having cross-section representation. It will end in a situation where only privileged classes will be representing the people in parliament and I do not want to see that.
I do not want to labour this, but I do want to say that I agree 100 per cent with the

This is a measure which is in the interests of all members of the house, and, if I may say so without being misunderstood, in the interests more particularly of the opposition members. vacant after all the casualties on the government side have been taken care of. Therefore I say we should not try to place responsibility upon the government for a measure so favourable to the opposition if there should be any criticism of it here or elsewhere in the country.
As one of the senior members of the house with some seventeen years' service, I merely wish to state that during that period of time -hon. members will probably know some of the personnel to whom I refer-I have seen men and women who have served the country long and well pass beyond the portals of the parliament buildings after a general election, or forced to retire through ill health, only to return to a condition bordering on relative poverty. I do not think the people of Canada want that to occur in the future. In the last eight months or more I have talked to people about a scheme of this description. The hon. member for Peace River is perfectly right when he says there has been a good deal of discussion of the matter among various members of the house over many months. When I have gone to my constituency or have been talking to people elsewhere in Canada I have taken the trouble to say privately that such a scheme was being discussed by the members of the house, and I have not found any citizen, who has given any consideration to the matter and to the welfare of the membership of the House of Commons and of the country, who has uttered one word against a scheme of this description. I rose to say that my hon. friend spoke for us but as I was one of the three in this house who had given the Prime Minister the assurance that a substantial majority of our colleagues were in favour of such a plan I felt I owed it to the Prime Minister, yes, to the leader of the opposition, as well as to myself to say what I have just said.

I thank the Prime Minister for an eminently fair statement with regard to the leader of the opposition. As the senior member for the Conservative party on the banking and commerce committee, I wish to dissociate myself and the party from the remarks made by the two members from British Columbia. I do so with regret

because I feel that an agreement was reached by members and all party leaders on this subject. That is why I am particularly pleased with the statement the Prime Minister has made, and if I were to indicate that the Conservative party was not prepared in every way to accept full responsibility for agreement on this measure I would not be doing my duty as a member of the house and a member of that party.
We are responsible for our actions as individuals and as members of parties. We cannot delegate that responsibility to others. I take full responsibility for what I am saying and doing now. We as a party agreed to this measure and the huge majority of the Conservative party is in favour of it. The question of representation in this house is one of vital importance to the country. The calibre and quality of the people who can be induced to give up the best earning years of their lives to come here and serve the country is of paramount importance to the well-being of Canada. I say that as a professional man because I feel that the more professional men we can induce to take their places in this chamber the better the representation we shall have.
Under the present situation you cannot expect a professional man to give up his practice to come here. I do not care how carefully he works at his profession during the recesses and week ends, no man can be a member of this house and even do the necessary reading to keep himself up to date in any profession today in our modern world. Therefore we are virtually asking the professional man to give up his profession when we ask him to come here. If we are going to induce more people of that type to become members of parliament there has to be some small measure of security after long service. At one time in the thirties there were seven Canadians who had formerly held the high office of premier in various provinces and who were not then in office or members of any legislature. Of those seven four were in receipt of charity and one was on direct relief. If we are not prepared to look after those who, as a result of the judgment of the people in a free election, are called on to write and administer the laws of the country, we make a severe reflection on the whole status of our Canadian citizenship.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words-and I shall not detain the house very long-on the principle of the resolution now under consideration. As I do not belong to any of the political parties represented in the house, needless to say I have not been consulted. This enables me to express more freely my humble personal opinion.
I must say at the outset that I cannot approve entirely of the principle of this resolution. I should immediately add that I am not saying this with a view to gaining a political advantage; on the contrary, for the

Members of Parliament-Pensions proposal I would put forward might be even less popular, since it would provide for an increase in the indemnity to members of parliament.
Until now only senior members of the house have expressed their views on the matter; I hope that a junior member might also be permitted to express his humble opinion.
I simply believe that a higher and more adequate indemnity than is now paid members of the house would tend to improve the quality of the representation. I do not object to members who have served their country for several years receiving a reward; reward is probably not the right word. I should rather say that the public should be grateful to those who have spent here, as members of this house, say, 12, 15, 20 or even 25 years, for the very valuable services they have rendered to this nation.
I was listening a moment ago to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) who has submitted the most straightforward, but, at the same time, the most convincing arguments that I have heard in this house. Besides, the unanimous approval from the members proves it and reflects the general feeling of this house.
Mr. Chairman, this is what happens: A great many of the citizens of this country would be ready to offer their services, first as candidates, then as members, but they are prevented from doing so because of their responsibilities, as their financial situation would become a complete mess should they have to come here and represent their constituents during a period of four years.
I do not think that an uncertain pension, payable after 10, 12, 15 or 20 years, would be likely to improve their situation. On the contrary, if the members' indemnities were raised to $10,000 a year, they would be sure of receiving that amount and most of them could save say, $1,000, $2,000, $3,000, $4,000 annually and so accumulate a little fund which would help them to straighten out their affairs. Such would unfortunately not be the case so far as a pension is concerned and the young man who seeks a mandate would not be in a position to depend upon it when making up his mind. Granted he has been elected, he will be a member for four years afterwards. If he is defeated later on what will be the use of a pension he will never receive? What can he do?
Precisely because he has been away from his home for four years, a larger indemnity would allow this member, at least in certain cases, should he be, for instance, a professional man, or a small businessman, to pay somebody a salary, to a manager for example


who would keep his business going, who would see to it that his employees would give the best possible service. In this way the members' financial position would be protected until his return.
I therefore wish to say to all hon. members of this house-as a matter of fact I am just repeating what I was saying a moment ago- that I have absolutely no intention of making any political capital from this situation, since my suggestion will certainly be far less popular than the idea of a pension. All the same it seems to me that would provide a way to improve the calibre of the representation in the House of Commons. I am not a lawyer; of course, I would naturally like to be one but I have been denied this tremendous advantage. However, I wonder if a scheme could not be devised to allow the present senior members of the house, who are about to retire, to draw such a pension and to grant from now on a higher indemnity to the younger members who happen to be in the house at the present time and to all future members. Such a plan may not be feasible but if it were it would offer, in my humble opinion, a means of doing justice to the older members who have sacrificed themselves and it would tend to improve the quality of those who will seek in the future to represent their county in parliament.

Members of Parliament-Pensions say that I am probably the only member of the house who has a definite mandate on this question. It came about in this way. In a more serious vein, I should say that in view of the fact, if this legislation passes, that I shall be immediately placed in a beneficial economic position, I feel it would be more appropriate and more proper if I did not cast a vote, should this matter be brought to a vote.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for the second reading of Bill No. 390, respecting currency, the Royal Canadian Mint and the exchange fund.
Hon.	Douglas Abbott	(Minister	of
Finance): Mr. Speaker, as I explained at the resolution stage, the purpose of this bill is to bring together in a single measure a modernized version of our existing legislation relating to currency, coinage and the mint, together with the necessary provisions to continue and regulate the exchange fund when the Foreign Exchange Control Act is repealed.
The bill, as hon. members will have noted, is in four parts: part I dealing with currency and coinage; part II dealing with the mint; part III dealing with the exchange fund; and part IV providing for the repeal of old measures, and the coming into force of this new measure. I will say a few words about each of these parts in turn.
Part I provides a more up-to-date version, without significant change, of most of the provisions of the old Currency Act-the remainder of its provisions will be found in part II, relating to the mint, where they more appropriately belong.
The various clauses of part I, which are fairly technical, state that the monetary unit of Canada is the dollar, and then proceed

to deal with the denominations of our currency, the characteristics of gold coins and subsidiary coins to be provided, what constitutes legal tender and in what amounts, the currency to be used in public accounts and in contracts, and some other minor matters.
In this connection there are only three points to which I think I should make special reference.
First, in regard to subsidiary or token coins, which are defined in the bill as all coins with a denomination of a dollar or less but which, more technically, are coins which have a metal content less than their face value, in contradistinction to standard coins which have an intrinsic value as metal equal to their face value, the house will note from section 5 and the schedule that the same coins with the same denominations, the same composition and the same standard of weight and fineness are being provided. In the case of certain silver coins the remedy allowance is increased somewhat to the United States level, in order to make possible a more rapid production of coins.
However, we have also thought it desirable to provide for a situation which has arisen seven times during the last ten or twelve years, namely, that in war or emergency there may be a temporary shortage of some of the metals used for coinage-silver, copper, nickel-and it may be urgently desirable to conserve supplies of these metals for defence purposes. Hon. members will recall the various changes we have had to make in the composition of our nickel coin in recent years. We have had to make these changes under our emergency legislation. If this bill is enacted, the governor in council will in future have the statutory power to issue a proclamation changing the composition of any subsidiary coin when considered necessary to conserve some of these basic metals.
My second point relates to gold coins. In the old Currency Act there was authority to coin $20, $10, $5 and $2J gold coins with a standard weight and fineness which, at the old gold price of $20.67 per ounce, resulted in these coins having a gold content equal to their face value, and Canadian gold coins as well as British and United States gold coins were made unlimited legal tender for their face amounts. When in the mid-thirties the price of gold was raised to $35 per ounce, these coins had a metal content very much in excess of their value as coins. Consequently those held by private persons have tended to disappear from circulation. The house will realize that because at the present time we are not maintaining any fixed par for our monetary unit, it would be impossible to lay down at this time any fixed standard 55704-233
Finance Acts
weight for our gold coins, in other words, any gold parity for the dollar. Whatever may be the varying view of hon. members on this general subject of the so-called gold standard, I am sure all would agree with me that for the present it is, to say the least, impracticable to fix a gold parity for our dollar.
In this bill, therefore, we are simply trying to maintain the status quo. Section 4 provides that as and when the par value of the Canadian dollar has been established by or under an act of parliament and is being maintained, that is to say the par is being made effective, then the governor in council may by proclamation authorize the issue of gold coins with denominations of $20, $10 and $5, with a fineness of nine-tenths, and with a standard weight necessarily not specified but it must, of course, be such that the value of the gold contained in the coins is equal to the face value of the coins.
I may add that we have dropped provision for a $2.50 gold coin because at the present price of gold such a coin would be inconveniently small.
The third point relates to legal tender. The bill provides that a tender of payment of money is a legal tender if it is made in gold coins issued under the authority of section 4, which I described a few minutes ago; in subsidiary coins, up to certain limited amounts, issued for circulation in Canada or issued for circulation in any province of Canada before it became a part of Canada and which immediately before the coming into force of this act were legal tender in Canada; and, of course, notes of the Bank of Canada. As compared with the present legal situation, we are merely dropping the provision that British and American and Canadian gold coins issued in the past, on the basis of $20.67 gold, are legal tender for their face value; there is no longer any point in retaining this provision, as obviously these coins will not be turned over by a debtor to his creditor at their face value-certainly not except in the rarest of instances.
Part II of the bill brings together the provisions relating to the mint presently contained in part II of the Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act-part I of that act was repealed by the financial administration act passed last year-and certain provisions of the old Currency Act which are essentially related to the operations or functions of the mint.
This part provides that all coins of the currency of Canada intended for circulation in Canada shall be issued at and from the mint. It requires facilities for making coins and for the melting, assaying and refining of gold to be established at the mint in Ottawa-

Finance Acts
which is set up as a branch of the Department of Finance-and it permits the governor in council to establish an assay office or branch of the mint outside of Ottawa to provide facilities for melting and assaying gold or performing any other function of the mint other than coinage. Hon. members will recall that we have an assay office to perform these limited functions of melting and assaying gold in Vancouver, thus providing convenient access for gold producers in British Columbia and the Yukon.
The master of the mint and such other officers, clerks, and employees as are required are to be appointed in accordance with the Civil Service Act. The provisions of the old Mint Act protecting the retirement rights of certain old employees of the mint who were employed when the mint was a branch of the royal mint are being carried forward in this bill.
This part of the bill also includes the necessary provisions for the making of regulations governing the purchase of supplies of metal for coinage, the purchase, assaying, refining and storage of. gold, the prices, charges and other terms upon which the minister may buy, sell, assay, refine and store metals, the making of coins for other countries, and all other matters relating to coinage. It also includes detailed provisions for the trial of the pyx, requires the auditor general to inspect the store of bullion and coin at the mint at least once a year, and requires the master of the mint to make an annual report on the operations of the mint.
I now come to part III. The house will recall that when I announced last fall the dropping of all foreign exchange control regulations, I intimated that it would be necessary at this session of parliament to repeal the Foreign Exchange Control Act and provide for successor legislation suitable for the continuing conditions of the post-war period. The Foreign Exchange Control Act is one of the measures to be repealed by part IV of this bill.
To take its place we are proposing to re-enact in part III of this bill the essential provisions of the Exchange Fund Act of 1935 which it will be recalled was passed at a time of fluctuating exchange rates not too much unlike the present. The whole purpose of that act was to establish an exchange fund to aid in the control and protection of the external value of the Canadian monetary unit.
This fund was continued by the Foreign Exchange Control Act. Provision for its further continuance and for the conduct of its operations is contained in part III of this bill.
All gold, currency, deposits and securities now held in the account will, of course, con-

tinue to be held and the Minister of Finance is given power from time to time to purchase or acquire, or cause to be purchased or acquired, with money in the exchange fund account, the following: (a) gold; (b) currency of the United States; deposits in currency of the United States held in the name of the minister with the Bank of Canada or any bank designated by the minister; treasury bills or other obligations of the United States; (c) currencies of any country other than Canada and the United States that are freely convertible into gold or United States dollars, and deposits in such currencies held in the name of the minister with the Bank of Canada or any bank designated by the minister; and (d) securities of or guaranteed by the government of Canada.
The minister, of course, is also given power to sell or cause to be sold any gold, currency, deposits or securities purchased or acquired by him or on his behalf at any time with moneys in the exchange fund account, and the proceeds of the said sales, together with all earnings and interest, are to be credited to the account. The minister is also given power to make advances to the account out of the consolidated revenue fund on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve. Any expenses incurred in the operation of the account are to be paid out of the account.
As in the old Exchange Fund Act, the Bank of Canada is relieved of the obligation to maintain a minimum or fixed reserve ratio of gold or foreign exchange to its liabilities, and there are certain provisions designed to maintain the secrecy of the fund's operations. The provisions of the Financial Administration Act do not apply to the account, and while the auditor general must audit it and the transactions in connection with it, his certificate in general is limited to certifying whether the transactions in connection with the account have or have not been in accordance with the provisions of the act and whether the records of the account do or do not show truly and clearly the state of the account. No civil servant and no person employed in the Bank of Canada is permitted to allow any unauthorized person to have information in regard to the fund or its operations.
As I indicated at the time foreign exchange control restrictions were removed, it will be our purpose not to attempt to maintain any stipulated parity or fixed exchange rate for the Canadian dollar, at least under present conditions, but rather merely to operate so as to minimize extreme fluctuations-to smooth a trend somewhat rather than to attempt to resist a trend in either direction.

Part IV merely repeals the Currency Act, part II of the Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act dealing with the mint, sections 28, 29 and 30 of the Bank of Canada Act, and the Foreign Exchange Control Act; and provides for the coming into force of the new act on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council.
Perhaps I should explain that sections 28, 29 and 30 of the Bank of Canada Act are those sections which give to the governor in council power to require gold coin or bullion to be turned in to the Bank of Canada and to direct that in such a case the price paid shall be the old mint price of gold, that is to say $20.67 per ounce. The first subsection of section 28, which gave this power in respect of gold held by the chartered banks at the time of coming into force of the Bank of Canada Act, is already spent, and some other features of these three subsections relating to accounting are consequential in character.
I think it will be generally agreed that the primary effect of these subsections is to impose an unconscionable penalty and I think the time has now arrived when this penalty can be forgotten.
After the bill has been given second reading I shall move that it be referred to the committee on banking and commerce where the officers of my department will be available to explain its detailed and technical provisions.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few comments to make as I think the proper place to deal with these matters at length is in the committee. However, there are one or two matters to which I should like to refer. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will realize how fully we are in accord with him when he says that the intention of the government is not to try to fix any parity to the dollar at the present time but to smooth out the irregularities.

One question which I shall raise in the committee is in connection with the power being left to the governor in council to reassert it at their discretion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last night the hon. member for Kamloops had just concluded some remarks about tanks with respect to which I should like to say a word. I believe his point was that we should not have sent 17-pounder self-propelled guns with the 25th infantry brigade to Korea but that we should have ordered Centurion or Sherman tanks before and supplied them to the brigade. He referred
IMr. Adamson.]
to a statement he had made on this subject in 1950. In the first place I should like to say that a 17-pounder anti-tank gun is a normal part of an infantry brigade group, and the decision to send a number of these guns with the brigade to Korea was arrived at for purely military reasons.
When the brigade arrived in Korea the brigade commander found he was to be associated with United States forces but working as an independent brigade. The commonwealth division had not yet been formed, and that was one of the reasons which led him on May 6, 1951, to recommend that we substitute Shermans of the M-4A3E8 type for the M-lO's which are the 17-pounders. His message sent on that date to the chief of the general staff read in part as follows:
Because Centurions are not immediately available I have now decided to request permission to change the M-lO's for the M-4A3E8. Cost of these tanks would be much less than Centurions or Pattons. My decision has been made with the advice of British and United States armoured men and commander C squadron.
That was before the brigade group entered into action so that none of the hon. gentleman's remarks bearing on that aspect of the matter had any relevance whatever. The brigade entered into action with the tanks which they have since used and employed very well. There is only one remaining point and that is whether it would have been possible for us, even if it had been desirable, to have acquired either Centurions or M-47 or M-48 Sherman tanks at the time he suggested, namely, on the 7th of September, 1950. The answer is that neither Centurions nor Shermans of that type were available for us at that time. Later we ordered Patton tanks, the M-47, just as soon as they could be delivered to us. Subsequently production of those tanks was suspended and we ordered Centurions; and we are having delivery of the Centurions as early and as quickly as we could have done by taking the course as early as September, 1950, which the hon. gentleman suggested-if that had been advisable. We submit that it was not militarily advisable and it was not possible.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to leave the subject that is being dealt with at the moment and bring to the attention of the minister a matter upon which I asked him a question about two weeks ago. It comes under the heading of acquisition of buildings and works, one of the items under this section of the army.
What I have to place before him are a number of suggestions regarding the Yellow-head route that have been made by the Trans-Canada Highway System Association which has its head office in Edmonton. This organization, representative of urban and

rural communities in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, asks, now that the trans-Canada highway location has been definitely established as the south route- with which this organization has no disagreement-and having regard to the tremendous developments that are taking place in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, that in the interests of our national defence the highway between Winnipeg, Saskatoon, through Watrous, Saskatchewan, and thence through Edmonton and by the Yellowhead route to the Pacific coast should be proceeded with and a military defence road built either in co-operation with the provinces or directly by the Department of National Defence. I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and through you, sir, the minister, the representations made by these organizations and in particular a reference that is made in a letter of the 14th of May, 1952, wherein is embodied in short summary form the reason for the need of this highway. In that letter it is stated as follows:
In the case of a global war, northwestern Canada will very likely be one of the battlegrounds. Therefore, the Canadian National Railways must be supplemented-and with all haste-by a military highway in the same manner as the trans-Canada highway will supplement the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fact, northwestern Canada must have all three means of transportation-railways, highways and skyways. Even if the highways are knocked out at times as a rule they can be mended very much quicker and easier than railways.
I need not point out to the minister and the committee the development in northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba today in mineral production and in the production of uranium and other basic ores. That development makes northern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba one of the most strategic places in Canada. Indeed, the minerals being produced and the minerals about to be produced there will I believe, as years go by, forge the shield of freedom everywhere among the freedom loving nations.
I am not going to go into the details of the mineral development nor of the tremendous oil development in the province of Alberta. Suffice it to say that, in so far as oil development is concerned, although only about three or four per cent of the total area available for production has as yet been investigated, the oil potential is twice as great as that in Venezuela, one of the great potential oil fields in the world, and it is within seven billion barrels of that still remaining in the United States of America.
I could mention too the vast supply of uranium and of other basic ores. Today in the event that war should come there is no means of those areas being protected unless
Supply-National Defence there is available a military highway such as is suggested by the Trans-Canada Highway System Association supporting the northern or Yellowhead route. I want to refer particularly to some recent editorials on the subject and also to some speeches made with which I am in agreement.
One of the questions asked is this: Why is it that the federal authority has not been building military highways? And the answer given by the association is:
In case of war there should certainly be a military highway over the Yellowhead route to connect the cities of Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver and Prince Rupert and to supplement the Canadian National Railways.
On the 23rd of February, 1952, the Financial Post contained the following item:
There appears to be some difference of opinion in Ottawa as to what should be the policy on roads. Finance Minister Abbott has implied that they are relatively unimportant in defence and that their financing could not be undertaken at the same time as other defence needs. On the other hand Defence Minister Claxton is said to have admitted the inadequacy of the highway system. High army officers are reported to be alarmed at the state of the nation's roads.
Then it refers in the same issue of the Financial Post to the speech given before the Canadian Construction Association convention by president Robert Drummond in which he declared:
. . . that federal authorities have not fully recognized the vital importance of roads in time of peace or war.
Furthermore, a similar point of view was expressed by C. W. Gilchrist, managing director of the Ontario Good Roads Association who spoke in Toronto. He said:
The federal government's failure to recognize the importance of roads in defence is a policy which may, in the long run, prove hazardous to defence and detrimental to the well-being of the nation.
Again, the Financial Post, issue of February 15, states:
Mr. Gilchrist challenged a statement made by Finance Minister Abbott who had inferred that roads' are relatively unimportant in defence.
Then he goes on to say this:
Mr. Claxton said in the House of Commons that many bridges cannot carry the weight of even a medium tank. High ranking army officers have said that they are alarmed at the state of the nation's roads. Ottawa's plans for the proper use of roads and highway transportation in civil defence are also pitifully inadequate.
Finally, the Edmonton Journal of February 14, 1952, in an editorial dealing with Mr. Gilchrist's remarks, said this:
Of all highway projects none is more vital for Canadian defence that the evergreen highway from Winnipeg to Vancouver, of which the Yellowhead will be the western arm.
I want to add as well some of the views expressed by leaders in western Canada. The commissioner of the North Battleford board

Supply-National Defence of trade, Mr. Wright, set out the facts in a statement that he submitted to the department as to the vital need of this road for national defence. Mr. S. N. MacEachearn, commissioner of the Saskatoon board of trade, summed it up in these words:
Our highway committee has given considerable study recently to the problems of defence as they affect prairie centres. All across Canada citizens are being alerted to the need for instruction in civil defence in case war on a world scale again breaks out. Despite the efforts of leading citizens, many citizens in many of our cities are still apathetic. There seems to be a feeling that, as in the case of the last two world wars, Canada in the event of another outbreak, would still be free from invasion.
Then Mr. MacEachearn goes on to say this:
Canadians are now confronted with the possibility of an attack by a much more formidable enemy than the Japanese and by one at a much closer range. There is a feeling among citizens, particularly of the northern cities of the prairies, that there should be access to the Pacific coast and to Vancouver by a route additional to the ones now in existence. There may be a hurried need for the withdrawal of population from the Pacific coast to the prairies or for the supplying of defence equipment to coast points.
Then he goes on to point out that a highway such as this is necessary in the considered opinion of the Saskatoon board of trade, and the officials of that board of trade, many of whom had distinguished military records. The same applies to the Edmonton chamber of commerce and board of trade, and also to other boards of trade across northern Saskatchewan who are, as I find it, uniformly in support of action being taken in this regard.
A moment ago I mentioned something of the resources in northern Saskatchewan and Alberta as to minerals and oil. Let me also point out how necessary this road would be in connection with some of the defence projects that have recently been established in these four provinces. There is the vast aluminum plant at Kitimat, the estimated cost of which will be $550 million; an oil pipe line to Vancouver from Edmonton via the Yellowhead route, $82 million-the Yellowhead route follows in general the route of this oil pipe line; the chemical plant nine miles east of Edmonton, $54 million; the celanese plant at Prince Rupert, $24 million; the establishment at Edmonton of three new oil refineries, $20 million; the Sherritt-Gordon steel mills at Fort Saskatchewan, $17 million; the bombing site west of Cold Lake, $14 million; the new seaplane base at Lac la Biche, $12 million; a second chemical plant two miles east of Edmonton, $12 million. In addition to that, there is the establishment of the Greisbach barracks and ordnance depot at Namao, ten miles north of Edmonton, at a cost of $15 million. There is the housing


and equipment for 5,000 men at Wainwright camp, at a cost of $15 million.
In other words, there has been a concentration in the northern part of these four western provinces of defence works, without taking into consideration the development and the expansion in connection with the northern radar chain. I make this statement on behalf of these various boards of trade and chambers of commerce in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. I ask the minister whether or not consideration has been given to the building of this northern route as a military or defence project, having regard to the fact that billions of dollars' worth of necessary defence projects have been established in this area, and that in addition to that almost a billion dollars is now projected to be spent in connection with defence or quasi-defence projects necessary to the preservation of our freedom.

speechtext:
This matter was brought up in the house before, Mr. Chairman, and I answered the question on June 11 of this year. The answer appears at page 3125 of Hansard. I have very little to add to the answer then given. There is no such thing, that I know of, as a military road of the character described by the hon. member. There is a road, and roads are the responsibility of the provincial and municipal governments, with the single exception of the trans-Canada highway where parliament has appropriated money to assist in the project because of its national significance.
The Alaska highway was built as a military project because at that time it served no civilian need and could not be justified on any civilian grounds. For the same reason, that road has been maintained by the Royal Canadian Engineers as a military project, which it is. The Department of National Defence is interested in any improvements, in communications or transportation. It all helps. As for assuming any part of the financial responsibilities we would have to consider that in the light of other defence needs. We cannot do everything we want. We cannot do one-tenth of what we want with the money available, which has to be spaced out in the program. So far that program has not contemplated assistance to provinces or municipalities to do what the provinces or municipalities would do anyway for local and civilian purposes.
Now, I cannot add anything more to that. It is a plain statement of our position. We have not got the money to do it, and it is not our responsibility to do it. If we had more money for defence, we would apply it on more urgent military needs than this one.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
I welcome the statement of the Minister of National Defence, because I know he realizes how important the defences of the west coast are. As the member for Nanaimo has pointed out, he feels that perhaps there has not been the same consideration given to the west coast as there has been to various other parts of this country. I am not going to say that is true. I am very pleased with the development of the great airport at Comox, which has been proceeded with by the minister, as well as the one at Tofino. At this stage, I should like to express my personal appreciation of the assiduous attention the minister has paid to his job. I do not think there is any minister in the cabinet who has had a bigger job or who has worked harder.
The minister mentioned the fact that the road systems of this country are the primary responsibility of the provinces. I believe that all hon. members can agree with that. However, I have often thought that with the tremendous sums of money we are spending in national defence for the establishment of these various projects, it might be well if the minister were to approach the provincial governments to see if there were any joint projects into which they might enter on a basis of mutual profit. I recall a very important road that has been suggested since 1943. As a matter of fact, it would link up the airport at Tofino, which is a defence airport, with the road system of Vancouver Island. The road would be about 30 to 35 miles long, and would cost something over $1 million. I believe the hon. member for Nanaimo was the officer commanding that area at the time it was first contemplated. Whether or not he has changed his mind since then, I still believe that it would be a valuable and important road. I like to think that if such a road were established it would not be entirely a capital investment with no profit, because after all if the minister will look over the record of the cost of transporting equipment, supplies and personnel into the Tofino airport during the war, he will find that it amounted to a substantial figure. One might offset the million dollar expenditure for that road against the continuing cost of moving supplies in and out. I think the minister might find that he had made a good bargain by investing that million dollars.
I should like to point out also that to get personnel and equipment into the Tofino airport during wartime it was necessary to send convoys down there. Fortunately we did not have an instance such as that at Estevan Point 50 miles north, where a Japanese submarine shelled the coast during the war. But actually, to move troops in there with any safety by water, convoys would have to be provided at considerable expense. I would
Supply-National Defence .therefore strongly urge the minister to ask his officials to look into the possibility of establishing that road. After all, not only would it be of great military worth but I think that the province could easily be considered as going in on an economic basis with the minister and assisting him.

speechtext: Will the minister give us some explanation with regard to this new service college that he intends to establish in Quebec, according to his statement made on Thursday, June 12? speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so. The purpose of this college is to supplement the officer training facilities we already have either at Royal Roads and the Royal Military College at Kingston, the Canadian services colleges, or at the universities and in other plans. In order to meet the particular needs and circumstances of the province of Quebec and of Canadians of French-speaking origin we have decided to establish a Canadian service college at St. Johns in the province of Quebec. It will be located in the present army barracks which are being substantially added to and renovated.
The intention is to open this college, in the first instance, for one year when students having the equivalent of junior matriculation will be brought up to the equivalent of senior matriculation, which is the requirement for entrance to Royal Roads or R.M.C. and is also needed for entrance to most universities in order to take a course having technical qualifications such as that of engineering. If the success of this operation warrants it, it would be our intention to carry on this particular college for a second and third year so as to have it on the same basis as R.M.C. and Royal Roads.
I should add that only a small proportion of the officers who enter the armed forces come from the services colleges. By far the greatest number do not come from college at all, but come in by direct entry, on short service commission or for aircrew in the air force. The second largest group comes through the universities, through the university training plan. It is only the third group that comes from the services colleges. We want the largest possible proportion of men coming from the services colleges to have technical qualifications, particularly as engineers or other classifications requiring

Supply-National Defence similar educational qualifications. That is a main justification for having Canadian services colleges.

speechtext:
In the
first session of this parliament I pointed out the requirements for defence with regard to a highway which was under consideration in this chamber at that time and which was known as the trans-Canada Yellowhead route. In view of the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre I take this opportunity to draw the attention of the minister to the views that I expressed at that time. I believe they are as applicable today as they were then. Irrespective of a highway of national importance to serve the needs of the population, I believe that a Yellowhead pass highway would serve and meet the defence needs; I refer to a highway into Edmonton from the east and west of Edmonton through the Yellowhead pass. Were money made available, and consideration given to its early construction, I believe it would meet the defence needs. I am sure the minister is well aware of the situation with regard to representations that have been made from time to time to the effect that a defence highway in and out of Edmonton would serve the needs of the future and would also serve the defence needs for the present. I hope that every consideration will be given to some means of having that highway put over the Yellowhead route. It would serve not only the greatest number of people in western Canada and our defence forces but would be for the greatness of Canada in the years ahead.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext: I appreciate what the hon. member for Edmonton East has said. I think he was the first to speak to me about this, and also about the highway to connect Edmonton with the Alaska highway. Hon. members from every province have made similar representations at one stage or another about roads in their provinces, and very good cases can be made for them. I can think of several in the maritime provinces, for example, as well as in Newfoundland and British Columbia, in fact in every part of Canada. But these roads are primarily for the use of the provinces and their inhabitants and, as such, are a provincial responsibility. If there are very unusual circumstances, where a highway would not exist and would not be practicable except for federal support, and if such a road were considered essential for military operations, then of course the situation would be different. But we do not know of any such road among those thus far suggested.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am in accord with what has been said by the hon. member

for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Edmonton East with respect to the Yellow-head highway from Winnipeg to Edmonton and the northwest. I have spoken on previous occasions with respect to this highway, and I wish to state again, I hope this will be given serious consideration. I contend that highway No. 5 between Winnipeg and Edmonton is the link between the east and the great northwest. The hon. member for Lake Centre has referred to the many millions of dollars invested in the city of Edmonton, but there are one or two spots he may have missed. I would refer again, as I have on other occasions, to the oil fields in the Lloydminster district. There are two refineries there, and a new plant was built last year by the Sidney Roofing Company. There is a great amount of bunker C fuel oil going out of these fields in the Lloydminster area, as well as a large amount of asphalt.
Not only should we look upon this as a defence highway, but I believe it would pay dividends by the future development of the northwestern part of this country, commercially. As I said before, this is the real link. No chain is stronger than its weakest link, and I believe this link would strengthen our defences, as well as bolster the economy between Winnipeg and the vast area around and northwest of Edmonton.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am interested in this matter. Only a couple of weeks ago when the estimates of the minister in charge of federal highways were before the committee, I made reference to it. At that time I brought the Yellowhead pass route to the attention of the minister, pointing out that it would be important as a defence project, and asked him to bring it to the attention of the Minister of National Defence.
I hope the Minister of National Defence will realize that all defence projects are not necessarily located in this part of the country. This is a big country, and a potential enemy might use roads farther west. The project mentioned by the hon. members for Lake Centre, Edmonton East and The Battle-fords would take care of a problem out there. I wish to associate myself with the remarks of those hon. members.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one further reference to make. Apparently the minister has put a complete damper on the possibility of consideration of this matter. Let me point out to him that in the winter of 1950 the chief of the Canadian general staff pointed out, as it is reported, that the Jasper highway and its continuation through the Yellowhead pass to the Pacific coast is of high importance, to quote his words, "to the defence of Canada and the marshalling of 55704-234
Supply-National Defence military forces for the Pacific". The attitude taken by those who apparently know what the necessities are is that the chief of general staff was stating but the simple truth when he referred to the need of this highway as a strategic military highway. That fact has been accentuated by the development I tried to point out.
When the hon. member for The Battle-fords suggested that I had neglected to refer to the oil fields at Lloydminster, perhaps he had not noted that my reference was not to the oil fields of any particular province. I realize that the development at Lloydminster was the first in the northern Saskatchewan or northern Alberta area. It was of course included when I stated that, while only a small portion had as yet been surveyed, the potential oil supply was little less than that of the United States. The information is that at the present time the potential oil supply is about 20 billion barrels, as compared with a potential still existent in the United States of 27 billion barrels. Certainly I had Lloydminster in mind, though I did not specifically mention it. My reference was to oil developments generally.
While the minister has spoken as if this were a provincial matter, my personal belief is that it is a development necessary for our defence. If we are going to develop the northern parts of Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba and British Columbia, then in the absence of an adequate military highway we would find ourselves in a serious situation if -and God forbid-we should ever find ourselves in a war. Certainly in the light of the vast potentialities and developments in that area, there is no comparison between the requests and demands for this highway as compared with the demands for highways in other parts of this country where the development does not serve the potentialities now apparent in those four provinces.

The United States has not left the whole matter of strategic highways to the states of that great country. They recognized long ago the necessity for integrating their highway system with their defence problem. In that country the federal government has proceeded not only to build a number of trans-United States highways, but they have gone further and have contributed substantially to a network of secondary highways within the states.

Supply-National Defence
It looks to me as though many of our defence preparations would be rendered useless, or at least greatly minimized in their effectiveness, if we do not have ways of transporting overland some of the equipment that would be required at given places and times. If there is any doubt as to where responsibility lies, then it would seem to me to be wise for the federal authorities to confer with provincial authorities in an attempt to integrate the highways for defence requirements. I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre and others who have spoken this afternoon have made a strong point, and I support them in it.

The reserve army strength has increased by over 13,000 since March, 1948, to a present total of approximately 47,000. Despite the fact that 5,000 members of the reserve army joined the active force in 1951 . . .

I think that statement is likely to create something of a wrong impression because it happens that 1948 was the year in which the strength of the reserve forces, including the army, was at the lowest level that has ever existed. If one looks at the report of the Department of National Defence for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950 one sees that on page 88 the strength of the reserve and active forces is listed. The strength of the reserve army in 1925-26 was 49,000 and by 1927-28 it had risen to 52,000. From then up to 1935-36 the strength remained in the 50,000's. In 1935-36 there were only 45,000, and just before the war the figure rose to 51,000. During the war of course their number greatly increased, so we will have to leave that out of consideration. In 1945-46, however, the figure was 56,000, in 1946-47 it was 37,000 and in 1947-48 it was 33,591. Then the figure rose until in 1949-50 it was 43,047.
I mention that because I think as the sentence in the white paper stands now it gives a wrong impression as to the way in which the strength of the reserve forces has increased. It gives the general impression that the increase in numbers has been extraordinarily good. I think one of the weaknesses in our entire set-up is the relative weakness of our reserve forces. It has been my opinion ever since I have been a member of the house that not enough attention has been paid to our reserve forces and particularly to increasing their strength so the units will have enough men with whom to carry on adequate training. Would the minister give the committee an explanation of the present position with regard to that force which was to be known as the Canadian Rangers? As he knows, during the second world war a force was established in British Columbia known as the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers which did excellent work. The units were located in the rural areas of the province where there were no reserve force formations, and I think at one time over 10,000 belonged to the rangers. Their esprit de corps could not have been higher. Most of the members of the force were not of an age to be in the active forces. They were mostly men who understood getting around in the rural areas of the province, and they did a grand job. I do not think the minister will question that fact.

Supply-National Defence
Some years ago it was indicated that this force was to be reconstituted, but very little progress seems to have been made. In fact I am wondering whether the idea has been abandoned. If that is the case I think it is a great mistake, because many of these men who did such good work during the war are prepared to carry on. There are functions for them to fulfil. For example, some of their functions were to assist in repelling any invader, to assist in anti-sabotage precautions, to assist the active forces in the isolated areas of the province, to do coast watching and to report any unusual occurrence. I believe that the numbers allowed for these formations are so small that it is going to be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to establish the units again.
I hope the minister can assure us that the intention is to drive ahead with this plan. There were to be units not only in British Columbia but also in the Northwest Territories and possibly in the Yukon. I believe there is a great work to be done. One aspect of the matter is that these units had a great influence on the young men in the districts. They got young men to join the active forces. They built up morale throughout the districts where the units functioned. Will the minister tell us the present situation with respect to this force?

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext: The force was reconstituted some four years ago under the name Canadian Rangers as an element in the reserve militia, and organization has been pressed forward. It was never the intention to secure a large number of men in any one locality. The object was to cover as far as possible every isolated part of Canada, and there are units in virtually every community in the more isolated sections of the country. I have seen maps showing where they are located, and I would be glad to have one shown to the hon. member from which he would see that there is very wide coverage not only of the coast of British Columbia, and to a lesser degree the Atlantic coast, but also the Yukon, the sub-Arctic, the Arctic and other localities where there are no other forms of organized police or military formations. Our object has not been to build up large units. We thought if that were done the men would get browned off and the effort of organization and maintaining interest would far outweigh the usefulness of the results obtained. On the other hand the object was to secure an organization of key personnel, and I believe that has been done.
