During the past twelve months the recruiting for the women's division of the R.C.A.F. has been opened up. I want to raise a question with regard to the discipline of that force, and I refer particularly to the attitude of the service towards the women in it. I think I can best illustrate my point if I refer to a detailed case, but I would prefer to do so without mentioning the name of the party concerned.
A young lady who was brought up in a Victoria home recently joined the women's division of the R.C.A.F. She was posted to Aylmer, and during her service had written continually to her relatives in Victoria. Suddenly, on April 10, those letters ceased to reach the relatives. After a long period during which their own letters were not replied to and telegrams were not answered, they became very concerned about the whereabouts of this young lady. They therefore communicated with the chaplain on the station at Aylmer, Ontario and on May 17-please note the date, May 17-they received word that this young woman was absent without leave.
In the letter from the commanding officer he advised the relatives that the security police had been notified, and then he went on to use these words:
No further action was taken at this point, as it would be a waste of the taxpayers' money.
3704	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
Then he went on:
The practice of personnel absenting themselves without leave is not unusual in the service, and not too much weight is placed upon these actions,
I hardly like to put on record the words which were used by the relatives of this young woman, after suffering terrible distress during this period of her absence and then being told that further action would be a waste of the taxpayers' money. It certainly caused them terrible heartburnings, because no matter what value the R.C.A.F. might place* on this young woman, her relatives' affection for her certainly could not be assessed in dollars and cents. I quote from the letter from the relatives:
This young woman must be found no matter what the cost may be to the taxpayers. We have paid taxes for more than thirty years, and we demand this protection and consideration. In any case, whatever of suffering or misfortune has overtaken her, we hold the R.C.A.F. responsible. We feel that they have been guilty of gross neglect and brutal indifference regarding the welfare of our dear girl who was placed under their authority.
Personally I can think of no statements which could be made by a commanding officer which would show less consideration or be more brutal than to tell the relatives no further action was being taken because it was a waste of taxpayers' money. I know that is an isolated case; but I do think that, at a time when we are just taking women into the services, if the attitude expressed by that commanding officer is also the policy of the department or the general attitude of the R.C.A.F., then there must be a change in that attitude if the women's division is to attract the right sort of young women. While it may quite possibly be the attitude of some of the services in so far as a man is concerned who goes absent without leave or becomes a deserter, that is good riddance to bad rubbish, that attitude must not exist so far as the women in our services are concerned.
I feel that if a real effort had been made to locate this young woman, who to date has not been located in spite of inquiries I have made personally through the various police forces, surely the first people to communicate with would have been her next of kin. I do feel there may have to be a somewhat different attitude adopted, so far as the women's services are concerned, to that which is normally adopted with regard to a man. A man may go absent without leave and there is probably every justification for not notifying the parents or the next of kin about him; but where a young woman is in the service I cannot help feeling that a different attitude must be adopted. The first action to be taken should be to notify the next of kin that a girl is either absent without leave or cannot be accounted for.
IMr. Pearkes.]

There is just one paragraph in the letter from these people which I think describes the mental anguish that they are suffering. It reads as follows:
Naturally, we fear that some dire calamity has overtaken our girl. She may be in dire need, and any number of dreadful things may have happened to her. This long silence from one who has always been so kind and considerate is very hard to bear and impossible to understand.
I am quite certain the minister will appreciate the anxiety of these people in this case. I am not raising any point about the particular case. I am simply saying that at this time when we are taking women into the services there should be a careful review of the attitude of the services towards the women for whom the senior officers are, in some measure, responsible.

With regard to the radar stations, the manning is beginning. The commanding officers of the stations are beginning to take up residence, and some men have arrived. The operation is therefore beginning and will be carried on during the summer.
With regard to the ground observer corps, this has recruited about 35,000 personnel. Filter centres are being set up at a number of points which may later be increased. Detachments of regular force personnel are being located at these points to provide a permanent nucleus and to organize and activate the corps in their respective areas. All the top civilian positions have been filled with volunteers. Despite the fact that no national call for volunteers to serve as spotters has yet been made, applications have been received from enough persons to fill about 65 per cent of the positions required at the outset which will number about 75,000. Consideration will be given to the timing and the extent of further expansion.
The main purpose of this corps, as the hon. member knows, is to supplement the R.C.A.F.'s early warning chain by reporting
Supply-National Defence low flying aircraft seen or heard and aircraft in distress. The organization and the control of the corps is the responsibility of R.C.A.F. air defence command which also controls the early warning system. The air defence command is working closely with the other armed forces, R.C.A.F. association, air cadet league and civil defence officials in setting up the corps.
There has also been good co-operation from the provinces and organizations that employ people like fire rangers and the like. Reports from the observer posts which are to be set up would be funnelled in by telephone, telegraph and radio, which would pass on the information to the proper R.C.A.F. authority. This corps is to be organized so that in the event of an emergency it could provide a 24 hour service. But its peacetime activities will be limited to training exercises involving R.C.A.F. aircraft.
This is quite an experiment in a country having the low density of population that Canada has and we are proceeding step by step with the experiment. As the hon. member sees, it is being brought along.

Perhaps at this point I should answer one or two points raised by the hon. member in his opening remarks concerning airfields in Europe. As reported at page 3646 of Hansard he said that the danger of the lack of airfields was brought to my attention many months ago by the leader of the opposition who, at the last session of this parliament, called attention to the lack of technical troops in Europe and advocated the provision of engineer units which would assist in the construction of these necessary airfields in France and Germany.
The leader of the opposition did make that suggestion; but I do not think he referred to the danger of our not having airfields. In fact, as I remember the discussion, his observations were almost surprise at my having stated that we would need airfields in Germany.
I would point out that engineers, and particularly service engineers, are the class of men of which perhaps we are in shortest supply in Canada. We have an acute shortage of service engineers in this country. There is no shortage in Europe of civilian tradesmen, including construction engineers and the like. So it would be most uneconomical and wasteful for us to send engineers from Canada to do this job in Europe, particularly as I believe a rather moderate estimate would be that a Canadian would cost about five times as much per day to do the same amount of work as a European. It would be somewhere between five and ten, I would think.
With regard to airfields, our difficulty is to get the North Atlantic Treaty Organization through SHAPE to allocate to us airfields which it would be possible for us to use. That allocation has been made in respect of two airfields in France and two in Germany, but the location of only one, in France, has been formally settled. Arrangements have been made with the French government to handle the construction of that airfield, as was announced in the house some time ago. I understand that these arrangements are capable of being extended to other similar developments in France. In this I think we
Supply-National Defence are a bit ahead of some other countries which have not yet made any arrangements whatever.
The arrangement is quite satisfactory. Under its terms the French government are calling for tenders for the construction of the necessary works at the airfield near Metz. The contractors are taking a good interest, and the matter is being handled in a businesslike fashion. When tenders are received they will be considered by representatives of the French government, of the Department of Defence Production and of the R.C.A.F. working together. The Department of Defence Production and the R.C.A.F. will be represented at all stages and will exercise the closest . possible supervision over the awarding of contracts and the execution of the work.
The situation in Germany is still unsettled. As hon. members know, the state of occupation is being brought to an end and in consequence the operation of the occupation agreement. This is not the best time at which to negotiate either with the British, French and United States authorities or the German government. However, these negotiations are going on steadily and I expect will reach a satisfactory conclusion. The delays for which we were not responsible have postponed the construction and use of these air stations by several months.

527. Departmental administration, $2,217,425.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to make any extended remarks at this time on this item. We have had a veterans affairs committee and we have discussed there matters having to do with the affairs of veterans. The main problem that has concerned veterans for the past year or so has been the question of war veterans allowances. As hon. members well know, this subject was dealt with by the veterans affairs committee and by the house a day or two ago. Whether or not it was dealt with satisfactorily is a question for the veterans themselves across the country to determine. Some of us felt it had not been dealt with very satisfactorily but it is a matter of history now, and I have no intention of saying anything further in that connection.
With respect to the work of the department in general, I would think that by now it must of necessity consist of a more or less routine carrying out of the provisions of the veterans charter which has been in effect for the last five or six years. The veterans of the second world war no doubt are well rehabilitated by now. So far as student veterans at our universities are concerned, I believe the university courses taken by different ex-servicemen are now completed, and I do not think it is out of place to say that I am sure the people of Canada have been well pleased with the splendid record made by the young men who took part in the second world war and who have taken university courses. They have shown that they can more than hold their own with students from civilian walks of life.
Another big rehabilitation problem that has confronted the department and the government has to do with the Veterans Land Act, where the success of the government perhaps

has not been as great as in the case of education. I am not going to dwell on that point at the present time. In general I think the hospitalization of veterans has been very acceptable to the people and that the veterans themselves consider they have been well looked after. There' is one problem that I think concerns us all and is of very great concern to veterans throughout the country.
I refer to the matter of housing. It is not my intention to go into the question to any extent today realizing of course that perhaps it is only a problem of the veterans affairs department to a very small degree. However,
I know the department is very much interested in it, particularly in view of the fact that 60 per cent of the people looking for houses in Canada today are veterans. It might interest hon. members to know that in Canada at the present time there is a shortage of some 700,000 housing units affecting an estimated two million people. This is a very serious situation indeed and one which is of great concern to veterans all across the country.
There are many reasons why the problem is not being solved more readily. One is the great shortage of building materials throughout the country. Another is the increase in the rate of interest for those who have to borrow in order to build homes, and the third is the scarcity of labour. I need not dwell on the necessity of houses. As I said a few moments ago it is a problem of which we are all aware and which we all understand. A house is the foundation of the home, and the home of course is the foundation of our society. In this connection I should like to read a paragraph from a report of the dominion housing committee of the Canadian Legion. The report is issued under the name of T. A. M. Hulse, chairman of the Legion housing committee, and in it there is the following:
It is not an overstatement to point out that the moral basis of our system and our national security even, as well as health and welfare standards, could be influenced adversely by poor housing conditions. One of the leaders in social work study of the Toronto university has said: "Housing is the basic factor which underlies most of the problems which are faced by health and welfare organizations in this country. If we can do something about the housing problem we might actually do a great deal to reduce efforts dealing with problems of public and private welfare. Federal social security programs are now more significant than ever. These will continue to be frustrated in large measure by this basic underlying shortage."
As I said a moment ago, I do not think it is necessary to dwell on this very serious problem. I simply call it emphatically to the attention of the house, the people of the country and the different governments and departments of government throughout
Supply-Veterans Affairs Canada. It is a most serious problem so far as veterans are concerned, and I hope something will be done to improve the situation in the coming year. There are other matters which might be discussed at this time, but we can discuss them as the items come up.

I should like to say a brief word about the patience of the officials of the pensions and war veterans allowances branches. I have given them some pretty bad cases to handle, and I must say they have handled them with outstanding patience and with satisfaction to the veterans and their wives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Following the difficulties which took place in the Charleswood settlement and in St. Vital last spring as a result of freezing of the septic field, an undertaking was given by the department to make a survey, once conditions had been restored to normal, with a view to discovering whether or not the fields were properly laid, whether they had been properly maintained, and what caused the difficulty; and to determine what it might be possible to do to take care of it.
Within ten days I had a report by telephone that the examinations in those fields were taking place. I believe they began in Charleswood and were then going on to St. Vital. I am not certain as to which place they began, but that examination is in the process of being made. I am told that the fields which are being examined are test fields suggested by the tenants themselves- that is, by the occupants of the houses themselves-and that they are proceeding at the present time. We are awaiting a final report as to what the discoveries were. I believe the original commitment was to test five of these fields in each district in the presence of and in circumstances suitable and agreeable to the occupants of the houses. That is proceeding and we are anticipating a report shortly.
Is it the case that the department has employed Mr. Scott, the water engineer who laid out the system to begin with, to give advice?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: At the time we committed ourselves to making an examination, the first suggestion which was made by the department as to officials to give expert opinion on it was as the result of a question by some of the veterans concerned. They wrote to the department-as a matter of fact, they wrote to me-and asked whether it would be possible to secure the services of Mr. Scott who, as the hon. member knows, is retired. He was the former water district engineer and the man whose advice was sought in the first instance as being an expert in these matters. I consulted officials of the department and the minister, and consent was given to employing Mr. Scott if he was available. My understanding is that at the request of the veterans themselves he is being called in as consultant to pass judgment upon the efficiency or otherwise of the fields as laid out.
Carried.
Six o'clock.

Would the minister make the evidence available?
Supply-Veterans Affairs Mr. Mulch: When the report is available I will be glad to make it known.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I think item 548 stood at six o'clock and there was a question or two I wanted to ask. Can the minister state how many veterans are settled under the Veterans Land Act and what the situation is with reference to keeping up payments?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is that farming, or is the hon. member including small holdings?
Including small holdings. How many have kept up their payments in full; how many have kept up their payments in part and how many have made no payments at all during the past year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I doubt if we have the information in that form, but we can give you the number settled under the Veterans Land Act and the number in arrears.
There were 75,340 veterans who qualified; there were 55,464 who were approved for assistance, and there were 55,121 for whom disbursements have been made.
Have the payments been satisfactory? Perhaps the minister cannot give full details, but he could give some idea of the situation.
In full-time farming there were 4,023 in arrears out of 24,155 who have been settled.
Have any abandoned their holdings at all?

There were 37 veterans in full-time farming and 38 with small holdings whose cases have been referred to the provincial advisory board for consent to the recession of their contracts, as of March 31, 1952.

I notice that on page 589 a large increase in the number of settlement officers, grade 2, is indicated. There are now 223 settlement officers as opposed to 64 in the previous year, which seems to be an increase of three and a half times.

As will be noted on page 590, the over-all picture shows a decrease. The present total is 1,198 as compared to 1,209 last year. With respect to settlement officers, grade 2, it is due to a reclassification of these employees by the civil service commission. Similarly a little lower down on

Supply-Veterans Affairs the page under the heading "settlement supervisors, Veterans Land Act" there is a decrease from 209 to 46.

I noticed that, and I also noticed they were all grade 1 with a salary of $2,436 to $3,240. In this case they were grade 2 with a salary of $3,240 to $3,888. It does seem like quite a wholesale promotion.

The reason is that we have been endeavouring to get the best possible calibre of employee. The great majority of these employees are university graduates who have specialized in agriculture, and naturally we have to pay to get the better class of man.
They were already employed?
Not all of them, though most of them were. I am informed that many were threatening to leave the service unless a reclassification was made.

Item agreed to.
550.	To provide for the payment of grants to veterans settled on provincial lands in accordance with agreements with provincial governments under section 35 of the Veterans Land Act, 1942, as amended, and payment of grants to veterans settled on dominion lands, in accordance with an agreement with the Minister of Resources and Development under section 35 of the Veterans Land Act, 1942, as amended, $600,000.
I should like to ask the minister where these settlements are in the different provinces.

The total number of veterans settled on these lands is 4,655, made up as follows: British Columbia, 146; Alberta, 2,056; Saskatchewan, 1,541; Manitoba, 422; 84 in eastern Ontario; 333 in Quebec and 73 in the maritime provinces.
Are these all on provincial lands?
Provincial lands and dominion lands.
In what form are the dominion lands?
There are some in Yukon, some in Banff national park and some at Whitehorse.

Under this item I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact, which of course he knows, that British Columbia is being developed at a very rapid rate. Provincial lands close to settlements are getting scarcer and scarcer. I suggest that his department should make a survey of the provincial lands available in British Columbia within a reasonable distance of small communities, get in touch with the provincial lands department and ask them to reserve any lands that are thought suitable. I find

that more and more men are becoming aware of the opportunities for settlement on provincial lands, but then they find they are too late because somebody else has bought the land.
I will be very glad to keep my hon. friend's suggestion in mind.

I do not know whether I am on the right item, but I should like to ask the minister whether he has considered further a question I have asked in the past regarding veterans whose small holdings are taken into cities. Will they be allowed to sell part of their property in order to save taxes? It is pretty hard on a man when his property is taken into a city, because taxes have increased so much.
There has been no final decision but the matter is being explored very actively at the present time, and there will probably be an announcement of policy in a short time.
I am very glad to hear that because in every city across the country veterans are in the same position, and they are very much affected by the burden of heavy taxes.
What are the veterans doing who have settled in the past on these lands? Are they small holdings? I take it they would not be farming?
They are small holdings.

The minister mentioned small holdings. I do not think I am quite in order in saying this, but I have been so busy I have had to be out of the house all day. In the interior of British Columbia it is very difficult for men to find two acres or more in the form of small holdings on which to settle. As the minister knows there has been considerable demand for the return to the requirement of only half an acre. It is a serious matter. Land is scarce, and I wish the minister would see that the regulation is changed so these veterans may settle on a small holding of half an acre or a little more. It is a very serious matter in my constituency. Over 250 veterans were denied the opportunity to settle on small holdings because of the increase from half an acre.

Are any of
these payments made in Newfoundland?

Yes, there are some settlements in Newfoundland. Some of the veterans devote their full time to their holdings, and there are some with small holdings who are engaged in commercial fishing. There are some settled on provincial lands also.

I wish to support the hon. member for Kootenay West. I think he has brought up a very important point. No doubt the minister has been giving a lot of consideration to it. British Columbia is peculiar-
In many ways.

-in the nature of its territory, and I think we have a different situation from any other province in Canada. The hon. member for Kootenay West has talked about the interior of British Columbia. What he has said is not only applicable to the interior but also to the lower mainland including my constituency of Burnaby-Rich-mond. We have a large number of veterans there who wish to settle on the land but the acreage requirement is too high. I support the hon. member for Kootenay West in bringing this matter to the minister's attention.
Has the minister given any consideration to these suggestions? I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond is quite right about the situation on the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I am sorry, I did not follow my hon. friend's question. What was it exactly?

Has the department given consideration to the suggestions advanced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond? I believe he has pictured a condition which certainly exists on the lower mainland of British Columbia.

We have considered the situation. Certain representations have been made at various times. I will keep in mind particularly the circumstances mentioned by the previous speakers with respect to British Columbia.

May I bring an example to the minister's attention and put a direct question to him. I do not expect him to answer now but I know he will consider it. Would the minister please investigate the situation so far as the riding of Burnaby-Richmond is concerned? There is a large amount of land which is mainly settled, but there are a lot of veterans in that part of the country who want small holdings. I should like to take this opportunity to ask the minister to have an investigation made by his officials and to let me have the answer as soon as possible.

Has the situation in this regard changed? I recall that close to Vancouver the department bought four or five farms, only one of which was developed. The other farms were resold, and that took place in
Supply-Veterans Affairs recent years. I assume if there had been a demand at that time the land would have been subdivided. Were the veterans requesting small holdings at that time? Those farms were sold. The department did not develop them.

As to the instance mentioned by my hon. friend, I am informed that the reason the project was not developed was that it was found it would have been uneconomical to do so in view of the high cost of providing the necessary services.

Item agreed to.
552. To provide for the reduction of indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement of a settler under the Soldier Settlement Act, in respect of a property in his possession, the title of which is held by the director, by an amount which will reduce his indebtedness to an amount in keeping with the productive capacity of the property and his ability to repay his indebtedness to the director, under regulations approved by the governor in council, $150,000.

Before this item is carried may I ask the minister a question. What is the position of the old soldier settlers under this item? He will remember that about thirty-three years ago there was an act to provide for the settlement of farmers and others, many of whom were totally unqualified to settle on the land, and I think the object then was to get those people out of the towns and cities. Some fifteen years ago I started a campaign to get those fellows clear title because I felt they had all paid in full at that time. Only three years ago did we get some action, and an amount of $150,000 was placed in the estimates. That has appeared annually so the people who were most in need could get their accounts straightened out. That has been some little relief and I see that a similar amount is in the estimates for this year.
In my opinion these accounts are not being cleared up fast enough, and I would like to know the position of these people today. The last figure I got, some five or six months ago, showed that they still owed an average of over $1,100 each. At that rate they will all be dead, and in some cases their families as well, before the estates get clear title.

Mr. Chairman, at the time this scheme of debt reduction was started, and I think the first estimate was in 1948, there were 2,637 active soldier settlement accounts with a total debt of $2,842,534.30 and an average debt of $1,077.94. As of March 31, 1952, there were 746 accounts with a total debt of $799,729.69, so my hon. friend can see that nearly three-quarters of the accounts which existed when we started this scheme in 1948 have now been closed. The average debt of the 746 accounts which now remain is $1,072.02. Included in the 746 accounts are

Supply-Veterans Affairs 225 in which reductions to a total of $108,821.77 have been approved on a time basis not exceeding three years. This leaves 521 of the original 2,637 whose accounts have not been adjusted. My hon. friend can see that there has been considerable steady progress in the settlement of these accounts.

Mr. Chairman, it may be rather remarkable that the average debt in 1948 was $1,077.94 and at the end of last March that average debt had only been reduced by $5.92. I think we are still getting a certain number of these people who are owing a lot of money to the department. From the last figure of $1,072.02 it is going to take a long time to get the debt squared up. Instead of $150,000 I would like to see an amount to take care of the whole thing and let these people get clear once and for all. They have done their bit for the country and now I think it is time for the country to do its bit for them.

Mr. Chairman, I know my hon. friend does not do it intentionally but the way he puts it does not give a true picture of the situation. It is true that the average debt has been reduced by only a few dollars, but I mentioned that of the 2,637 accounts which existed when we started this scheme more than three-quarters have been closed and settled. There are only 521 with whom there have not been adjustments. Their debt has not been reduced because these people have not paid.
It is all very well to say we would like to have just one large amount in the estimates and close up these books. However, in all fairness to all the other settlers who have met their obligations, and in fairness to all the veterans settled under the Veterans Land Act who meet their obligations, when there are cases of these older settlers who are quite capable of paying but who have refused to do so I hardly think it would be the proper thing to close out their account.
I know they are not in the majority but there are cases which I can quote to my hon. friend. There is one settler who, besides the land on which he was originally settled, owns land which is fully paid for and is valued at $17,000. He owns $15,000 worth of machinery which is fully paid for; and when he came to the supervisor and asked for an adjustment of his debt which was under $1,000 he was refused. But he walked out and bought a new car, and informed the supervisor that he was going away for a three-month holiday. I hardly think the parliament of Canada should be asked to close out that account.

It is rather a funny case for the minister to put up.
[Mr. Lapointe.3

All right; I can quote you some more. I mentioned that these might be extreme cases but I think the mere fact that cases like that do exist justifies the procedure we have been following over the last five years which permits the reduction of debt and a grant of full title to the men who deserve it and who are trying to do their best to meet their obligations.
We have odd cases such as the minister has quoted, but I can point out others throughout the country-
Tell us who they are.
It seems the wind is blowing through and there does not seem to be anything to stop it over by the curtains.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I think the minister might take this matter into consideration and clean up the mess. It has been a mess. We had the gentleman in charge of the department when this scheme was set up say it was a hastily improvised scheme to get these people out on the land. Having an admission like that from a gentleman who was there for a number of years prompts me to suggest that we might review the matter again.

I might add that when we are considering the supplementary estimates after the main estimates are through there is one vote, a dollar vote, covering this subject. At that time I will explain why the vote is there and my hon. friend will realize that we are even broadening the policy to permit more generous settlement of these cases.
I am glad to hear that.
Might I ask the minister what is the basis of payment. Does the department put up one dollar for every dollar the veteran pays, or just what is the scheme?

The debt reductions have averaged between 40 and 50 per cent. As a matter of fact of the amounts which have been reduced, and which I mentioned before, 45-56 per cent has been paid by the department and 54-44 per cent by the settler.
The soldier has to pay something himself.
Yes, we reduce his debt according to the new terms over a period of three years.

Might I ask what the terms of this indebtedness are? In the rather extraordinary case recited by the minister, has

the department no means of collecting such a debt? It would seem to me that would be the logical thing to do.

There are the normal legal steps that could be taken, but I do not think it has ever been done. I can just imagine what the reaction would be if at any time, even in extreme cases such as the one I mentioned, one of these men was evicted from his farm.
Is there any more fairness in allowing this debt to pile up than there is in writing it off?
We keep the title.

In the past there have been many cases where old men have been put off their land and other cases where settlers were compelled to sign quit-claim deeds. At that time the department had as director a Mr. Murchison who would have been much more in place working for some mortgage company instead of administering a soldier settlement scheme. I believe many more settlers would have been put off their farms if their treatment had not been exposed in this house.
There may have been such cases in the past, but there have been no evictions under the new scheme.

I should like the minister to
tell us the cost of administration of this particular project during the past year.
Unfortunately it is not kept separately, but is part of the whole cost of administration under the Veterans Land Act.

I want to support what the hon. member for Battle River has said. I think the cost of administration of this work should be kept separate. The case to which reference has been made is one of the extreme cases, and I know of many cases in the dried-out areas where the farmer cannot pay but the debt is still charged up against him. I am sure that the minister cannot refer to a case in the southeastern area of Alberta in which the same circumstances apply as the case to which he referred.
It does seem to me this is another matter that could be disposed of very easily. This is not the first time I have spoken in this house about old debts. The other evening I mentioned the subject in connection with another matter, but I know I would be out of order if I referred to it. Just because certain of these people are able to pay their debts does not mean everyone is able to do that. It depends entirely upon the circumstances, not only in the west but in the east as well. I think it is about time this matter
Supply-Veterans Affairs was given serious consideration and these old debts were cancelled.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
555. Post discharge rehabilitation benefits, including the training of merchant seamen and salt water fishermen pensioners, $3,677,500.

In this item what is meant by the training of merchant seamen-I know what that means-and salt water fishermen pensioners? What training and educational benefits have been given to salt water fishermen, and what fishermen in Prince Edward Island have had any benefit from that item?

I could not tell the hon. member how many Prince Edward Island men are affected by this vote, but it covers vocational training for these people. I am informed that at the present time we only have 190 veterans left in vocational training.

Are any
veterans in Newfoundland receiving benefits from this vote?
I am not sure if I have the information broken down by provinces. I shall look it up.

Under this section I should like to refer to a matter that has come to my attention on several occasions recently. It concerns the administration of the army benevolent fund. I trust I am in order in mentioning it here, because it is not mentioned elsewhere specifically.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is not administered by the department, so you will not find it in the estimates.

The army benevolent fund operates under an act which was amended the other day. It is administered by a voluntary board which reports through the Minister of Veterans Affairs to parliament. The annual report is tabled in this house, but the department has nothing to do with the administration of the fund.
Under what item or circumstances could one refer to the army benevolent fund?
You mean in the house?
Yes.
Well, there was a bill that came up the other day, and upon which there was a short debate.
Perhaps the minister could answer the question.

I would suggest that it might come under the item of administration, since
3718	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs the board must report to the minister. However, I have no objection if the hon. member wants to put a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member could ask a question and the minister will see if he can reply.

Briefly, the problem is this. Under the present set-up of the act only veterans of world war II are covered by the army benevolent fund. I understand that this is due to the fact the fund was created from amounts of money that were accumulated during world war II. The problem arises, however, with the increasing number of Korean veterans who are applying for benefits under this act. Those responsible for administering the fund must inform these Korean veterans that they are not eligible.
Upon making inquiries I find that the air force benevolent fund and the navy benevolent fund, which I understand are privately operated, have overcome the difficulty and apply the same treatment to Korean veterans as to veterans of world war II. They do it by a simple formula, in that they receive one per cent of all canteen funds. The information I have is that the only way the present anomalies in the army benevolent fund can be remedied is by government action. I am assured that the officers administering the fund are willing to take on this added responsibility, if there were a means whereby they could do so.

The hon. member is quite right in saying that only world war II veterans can benefit from the army benevolent fund. This fund was made up, as the hon. member knows, from regimental and canteen funds during world war II. He is also quite right in saying that the only manner in which the Korean veterans could be permitted to benefit from the fund would be through an act of parliament, because the board must necessarily administer the fund according to the act and the benefits are extended only to world war II veterans.
Each year the board makes recommendations to the minister, and as a result of those recommendations this year we had certain amendments to the act. I shall be pleased to discuss with the members of the board any further extensions which they might think appropriate.
While I am on my feet I might also answer the question asked by the hon. member for St. John's West with regard to the number of Newfoundland veterans who might have received vocational training. I am informed that at the time of union we took over sixty-two veteran trainees of Newfoundland who


had not yet completed their rehabilitation training. Of these, seventeen were being trained in Newfoundland, forty in other provinces, three in the United States, and the remaining two in the United Kingdom. Of these, sixty were being trained in universities and two in vocational courses.
Are they all finished now?
It is exceedingly difficult to say. I would not have that information. I would venture to say that most 'of the university trainees would be finished by now.

This item covers post-discharge rehabilitation benefits. For some time there has been a considerable amount of veteran opinion in favour of some action being taken to extend benefits of this type to the children of those men who lost their lives in the service of the country. For example, at the recent dominion convention of the Canadian Legion two resolutions dealing with this subject were passed. The first one read:
Whereas knowledge of resulting hardships encountered by widows and children of veterans of world war II who made the supreme sacrifice, when the age limit is reached and no further allowances are paid on behalf of the dependent children; and
Whereas it is desirable that the children be given an opportunity to continue their education and where the widow may desire to build a home or purchase new furniture, etc., for the benefit of her children:
Therefore be it resolved that all such entitlement and credits, etc., which the veteran would have received had he been spared to return be made available to his family.
There was a further resolution which read this way:
Whereas the widows of servicemen who were killed or who died during service will be unable to educate their children to the same standard which might have been attained had the father returned; and
Whereas it is in the best interests of the nation to have the rising generation well educated, particularly the children of men who died for their country:
Therefore be it resolved that the federal government be requested to instigate a policy for such dependents similar to that in force for single student veterans attending university or vocational training schools and receiving a monthly allowance under the Rehabilitation Act.
Following that convention the new president of the Legion presented a supplementary brief to the special committee on veterans affairs, as the minister knows. At page 5 of that brief we find this statement with regard to these rehabilitation credits. He quotes part of these resolutions I have read, and in addition says this:
The convention further indicated that it felt that the country, in memory of its war dead, could do something more for the family of one who died in service, and recommended that the rehabilitation

credits which would have accrued had the husband or father lived or some equivalent provisions be made available for his family.
Then after quoting the resolutions the Legion end their submission in this way:
These two resolutions are similar in purpose, and we are sure will commend themselves, both to the members of this committee and to the government. The people of Canada through their government would want to assume the obligation indicated in these resolutions, and see that these young people be assured of an opportunity for training and education which we may reasonably assume the father would have provided had he not laid down his life for his country.
In connection with this suggestion there are two features which I think merit consideration by the department. The first is that there was, of course, no liability to the country for the rehabilitation of these men who lost their lives. The second is that these children whose fathers were killed or who died in the service of the country are unlikely to have the same chance to obtain an education or to obtain a thorough training that they would have had if the father had returned to Canada. I believe that veterans generally are in favour of some proposal such as that suggested by the Legion. I would ask the minister to let us know the views of the department on this question.

The resolution was passed on to me by the executive council of the Legion and along with other resolutions it is now being studied by the department and will be considered by the cabinet. That is all I can say at this stage.

Item agreed to.
Soldier Settlement and Veterans Land Act-
561. To provide for protection of security-soldier settlement, and refunds of surplus to veterans, $25,000.
May we have an explanation of this item?
That is the usual vote for the settlement of veterans under the Veterans Land Act, to purchase property and so on. My hon. friend will see that there is also a supplementary estimate.

Might I point out that the purchase of property at Montney in the Peace river country for some 32 veterans has turned out successfully. This land was acquired from the Indian affairs branch, or at least from the Indians. It was reserve land. I think you have there an example that might be copied all over British Columbia and in many other parts of the country. Arable land owned by the Indians or reserve land not being cultivated could profitably be
Supply-Veterans Affairs taken over, as was done at Montney, and good prosperous homes could be provided for many of our veterans.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are four supplementary estimates to be found at pages 21 and 22 of the white book.
Pensions and other benefits-
816.	War veterans allowances-further amount required, $5,850,000.
May we have an explanation of this item?
This is to meet the increases which were provided by the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act.

Item agreed to.
817.	Gallantry awards-world war 2 and special force-further amount required, $3,000.
May we have an explanation of this item?
This is to provide for the payment of money for gallantry awards for the Korean force, the same as were given to veterans of world war II.

Has the government ever considered giving money awards to veterans of world war I for these military awards? I do not think they received the same consideration as that received by veterans of world war II or that which is being received by the veterans in the Korean war.

This matter was brought up before in the discussion on the estimates. During the first world war we were not paying; the British government was paying the monetary awards attached to these decorations. During the second world war we took over the payment of the awards that had been paid by the United Kingdom government in respect of world war I. Then during the second world war there were pecuniary awards given in connection with other decorations, which were not given during the first world war. We now assume payment for all. But we follow a uniform policy with the rest of the countries of the commonwealth as regards world war I decorations.

Has any consideration been given to Canadians who were imperial veterans of world war I and were paid in pounds sterling? Has there been any consideration of the fact that the pound sterling is so low in value?

I would not think that question would come under this item. These veterans are receiving disability pensions from the British government.

But due to the fact that the pound is so low in value they would not be receiving very much.
How many South African war veterans do we still have in Canada? I notice that we have a pension fund for them.
