330. Departmental administration, $584,997.
Is the Minister of Public Works making any statement concerning the work of his department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could make a real statement by reading what is in the estimate book. The Department of Public Works is not a policy-making department; we service departments, and we try to help every department of government as well as hon. members and people throughout the country who require public works. If it would please the hon. member I would be prepared to read the list of works we are undertaking, but I believe this would be an expenditure of time that would not be justified because hon. members have had this book of estimates for the last three or four months, and I know they are familiar with nearly every item. However, if they have any questions in

respect of any project I shall be ready to do my best to answer them.

Mr. Chairman, there is one feature about the department which gives me some concern, and which I think could be dealt with by the minister. I refer to the extent to which other departments of government are doing construction work.
I have had this matter in mind for some time, and I see by the morning press that the special committee of the Senate has made a recommendation on this same point. The dispatch I hold in my hand is headed "Ottawa is hit for by-passing Public Works". That makes it look as though the minister is being by-passed and we do not like to see that happen.
The report of the Senate committee has not yet reached us, but I have here the proceedings of the meeting of the committee where they cross-examined the deputy minister of this department. According to this press dispatch several definite recommendations were made concerning the Department of Public Works. The article sets out these recommendations:
(1) That federal government departments stop by-passing the public works department to build their own works. The report said this should be handled by the public works department, as the law intended.
Then the second recommendation deals with postage. The article then goes on to say:
Regarding public works the report said that departments other than the public works department plan to spend more this year than the $80 million budget of the public works department for this purpose.
Then follows this quotation from the report of the Senate committee:
It certainly appears this can have no other effect than duplication and overlapping and the inevitable general increase in costs that is bound to result from this practice.
Then the dispatch goes on to say:
Although provision was made in legislation for other departments to build their own works-
And again the article quotes from the report of the Senate committee:
-surely this was only intended to meet special circumstances, and was never meant to be used in the broad sense in which it is used today.
The hon. senators brought out during the course of their cross-examination the fact that public works were being constructed by the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. They refer also to canals being constructed by the Department of Transport, to the Canso causeway and to the airports also under the jurisdiction of that department. Then they make reference to armouries being built by

the Department of National Defence, though I think they meant the Department of Defence Production. There is reference to the new building on the Montreal road for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is being constructed by that corporation. There is further reference to buildings being constructed by the Department of National Revenue, to buildings by national parks branch, by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and to construction being done by the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Fisheries and by the commissioner of penitentiaries. I have only had time to glance through the report of this Senate committee rather quickly. I think other departments or branches of government are mentioned there, and it would look as though something of a raid is being made by other departments on the functions of the Department of Public Works. They seem to be wolfing the Department of Public Works.
This is really a serious matter because the Department of Public Works was set up, I think at the time of confederation, for the purpose of constructing public works in Canada. The department was entrusted with the construction of public works. I should like to know why that situation is being changed. It appears that under part II of the Public Works Act there is provision for another department to take away from the Department of Public Works the building of projects, and we have had many examples of this.	.
I raised this matter yesterday with the Minister of Defence Production. That department does all the building for the Department of National Defence, but that was not so before the second world war. Hon. members will remember that at that time defence building was done by the Department of Public Works. Certain forts were built in Vancouver, and if my memory serves me correctly they were built by the Department of Public Works.
Some weeks ago the Minister of Defence Production explained that his department was temporary, and it was hoped that eventually the work would be handed over to other departments. I would have thought that when that time came defence projects would go back to the Department of Public Works. When I asked the Minister of Defence Production about that yesterday he replied, as reported on page 3631 of Hansard:

The minister said a few days ago
that he did not expect the Department of Defence Production to be carried on indefinitely. I presume that in due course this work of building projects for the Department of National Defence will revert to the Department of Public Works? Is that the intention?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is a matter that cannot be predicted at this time. When the work handled by the Department of Defence Production becomes so small that it does not warrant the overhead of a separate department, the work will be placed elsewhere; but I cannot predict at this time where the work will be placed.
Apparently it is quite indefinite as to just which department will take on this work when the Department of Defence Production folds up. I am afraid that if this trend continues of having construction work done by different departments it will be more expensive than having the work done by the Department of Public Works. After all, the minister has trained men in his department and it has been their job for many years to build public works. I do not see why other departments should step in and take away that construction work. If it goes on the Department of Public Works will soon be in a position where it is not qualified to handle many of these projects. None of us would want that to happen. I do not believe the department is being given a proper chance at the present time, and I hope that the minister will put his foot down with his colleagues and see that these projects become the responsibility of his department.
Mr. Fournier, (Hull): Mr. Chairman, I am sure the praise and the encouragement of the hon. member in connection with the work of the officials of my department will be greatly appreciated. I was really flattered when I saw this Senate report where they indicated that all construction should come under the Department of Public Works. I would be the last to object to that. They indicate that more construction is going on outside the Department of Public Works than is done by that department, so I can visualize the department with a staff two and a half times as large as we have at the present time. I ask myself whether that increase would be justified when we know that most of the construction being done by other departments is of a temporary nature and may disappear within one, two or three years.
The hon. gentleman mentioned that the Department of Public Works was an old department of government. It was created at the time of confederation and has existed ever since. It has under its control all buildings and the housing of government services, and I am referring particularly to office space. Other departments have handled construction work. The Department of National Defence has always had an engineering staff in charge of the construction of barracks and other works which were never under the Department of Public Works.

Supply-Public Works
In former years practically all works along rivers and harbours were under the Department of Public Works, but then the national harbours board and other harbour commissions came into being and they undertook these works themselves. Then as to Indian schools, the Indian affairs branch has architects with special knowledge in these matters, and they are handling this construction. In the past this was handled by the Department of Public Works. In the matter of hospitals we do act for the Department of National Health and Welfare, as we do for many other departments.
My hon. friend should not fear that the Department of Public Works will disappear or that the officials in the department will not be able to handle any construction that is approved by hon. members in the way of estimates. Our present staff is not sufficiently large to handle all the construction work mentioned in the estimates. There is a shortage of this type of technical men and we cannot always undertake all the public works that are approved. They may drag on for a year or two, but eventually we are able to construct the authorized wharves, piers and breakwaters and do the dredging that is called for.	*
I think this department should avoid haste in the development of projects. I cannot change the mentality of the staff of my department. These men come in at an early age and are trained under a certain procedure and technique. It is often said that the Department of Public Works has the most red tape, and after ten years at the head of that department I think it is true. Hon. members may not realize how many reports must be made before a recommendation can be made to the treasury board and cabinet for authorization to present an estimate to parliament. For the sake of protecting the public I think it is good that we follow this procedure. Quite often hasty work is wasted work, and we pride ourselves upon having the most economical department in the government. This means that we have many revotes every session, but that in turn indicates that we have given a lot of thought and are ever aware of the responsibility which devolves upon us under the statute governing this department. I am always pleased to hear it said that certain works should come under the public works department. Nothing would please me more than to handle a good many projects, but I do not believe I could give satisfaction without increasing the staff. I think other temporary departments could do the work more expeditiously than it could be done by the public works department. The hon. member spoke of Central Mortgage

and Housing Corporation. I would not contest their right to put up their building. They must have experts. That is their line of business; but that organization did not exist when the public works department was created. It is another creation of government which has come about in modern times.
As to canal work, I think in the transport department they have people with special training who are capable of doing that work. I would not want to undertake to handle all construction work. Being a servant of the other departments and the public is quite difficult enough with the task we have now, because you would be surprised how many people are not satisfied with what we are doing. We are not doing it very quickly, so I think I would leave well enough alone as Minister of Public Works and do the best I can with the works we have to handle.
I am afraid the minister is a real Tory.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I beg your pardon; oh, no. That is the only word I object to in what the hon. gentleman has said.
I am afraid we have a real reactionary here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not what they say on my side.

After all, this department is meant to be the building department of the government. That is its job. The minister himself has pointed out that he believes the taxpayers get better protection from his department than they do from the other departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.
That is what it meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no; I did not say it and I did not mean it, so do not put a meaning on my words that I did not intend to give. Other departments are doing a wonderful job under the circumstances. I am trying to give the traditions of the Department of Public Works. We have certain traditions. It is not only the Tories who have traditions. They exist in other parties too.

The minister put it in this way. He said that his department gave great protection to the public. He explained what great trouble they went to in preparing their estimates. He told us all about the red tape and all the precautions to protect the public. Surely the public is entitled to just as much protection in the other departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Ask the other departments. Don't ask me.
I will be glad to help the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I don't need that help.
I am afraid the minister is getting an inferiority complex.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That may happen.
He seems quite prepared to sit back and let other departments kick him around. I suggest in all seriousness-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only man who has kicked me around is you.

The minister does not mind that. He kicks back, and well, too. I suggest in all seriousness that the present trend means the building up in other departments of staffs to carry on these building projects, adding an engineer here and an architect there, whereas that work should be done by the staff of the Department of Public Works which has facilities for doing these jobs. I believe no one would quarrel with the minister making additions to his staff so they could handle most of these public works projects. I do not believe there can be any question that there is bound to be duplication and waste of public money where you have a dozen or more different government departments doing their own building.

The minister was kind enough to say that if there is any project about which we wish to inquire now is the time to do so. I should like to tell the minister that we have an outstanding need in Fort William. I have been after the project for over twelve years and we are still keeping at it. I refer to a breakwater in front of island No. 2 for the storage of pulpwood and logs for our two large paper mills, our sawmills and the use of industry generally on that island. Two large delegations came here last March, and I expect their number will be doubled next year. All I want the minister to do is consider this as an important project, because we hope to get it next year.

I have spoken to the minister on several occasions during the past few months in an endeavour to ascertain from him what the government is going to do to prevent further deterioration of the Toronto islands. I have not yet had an answer from him, and I hope I shall be able to get one tonight. I have emphasized to the minister the essential part these islands play in the formation of Toronto harbour. I pointed out that without these islands, there would not be any Toronto harbour at all. 1 have also pointed out to him that the Toronto harbour is a very important part of the projected St. Lawrence seaway and that if the situation with respect to the islands is allowed to deteriorate further, the cost of repair in the years ahead will be many times more than it would be at the present time.
Supply-Public Works
Eventually that cost will have to be borne by the federal government, because harbours are a federal responsibility. I have talked recently with Mayor Lamport of Toronto, and he tells me that he is getting nowhere with the Department of Public Works. Frankly, he thinks he is getting the run-around from the minister. I should like to make a suggestion to the minister, who is a very practical politician. It is well known that the Liberal party would like to have Allan Lamport as its leader in Ontario, and he is pretty reluctant about taking on that rather thankless task at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That would not come under any item of public works, Mr. Chairman. I am sure of that.

I am just making a helpful suggestion. A very good way to persuade Mayor Lamport .to take on that rather unattractive task at the present time would be for the federal government to assist the city of Toronto with regard to the Toronto islands. I am trying to help the minister, who is a practical politician.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are not going to get me to choose the leader in Ontario. I have enough troubles in Quebec.
All I can do is make all the suggestions possible. I am simply trying to help the minister.
One mistake was enough.

As the hon. member for Peterborough West says, one mistake was enough. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would tell me, at long last, what the department intends to do with regard to assisting the city of Toronto in building protective works to help stop any further deterioration of the Toronto islands which, as I pointed out, are a vitally important and necessary part of the Toronto harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that the damage to the islands is caused by high water and floods-
Storms.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Storms-and that high water in a harbour does not do any harm. It may damage the islands, but the islands do not come under our jurisdiction at all. If we were to undertake to repair damages every time there was a flood or high water in the district I do not know if we could cope with the situation. I have said many times in the house that no district has suffered more from floods and high water than my own home city right across the river here. You see the Gatineau flowing into the Ottawa river, and every spring one-third of a town of about 4,000 people is flooded. When I was

Supply-Public Works
a member, before I became a minister in the government, I did make requests and pleas to get help for those poor people in Gatineau Point who were flooded. I never succeeded. When I became minister I had the dual capacity of member and Minister of Public Works, and I have had many discussions with myself as to what should be done for those people. If you are speaking about politics, and I know a little about that subject, I do not know why the member for Hull should not have had the best of the Minister of Public Works.
I am surprised that he didn't.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To date I have not convinced myself that it is any responsibility of the federal government; and if that principle is good in my own riding I think it should be equally good in Toronto. We have no jurisdiction unless it becomes a matter of a national disaster. When the municipality asks the province of Ontario for help in this direction, and when the province of Ontario will say: we cannot cope, the expenditure is too large, they can always come to the federal government and I am sure the federal government would consider any request from the province of Ontario under those circumstances.

I quite realize that every time there is flooding or erosion the federal government cannot be expected to right the situation. That would not be reasonable, and I have not appealed to the minister to do anything about the great losses and damage done to the shores of Toronto itself by erosion and flooding, nor have I appealed on a humanitarian basis for those who live on the islands, for property damage and so on. I am simply appealing on the basis that harbours, as I understand, are federal responsibilities. If this deterioration continues, then you are going to have no Toronto harbour. If you want to have a Toronto harbour as a vital part of the St. Lawrence seaway, it will have to be built up in the future, which will cost many, many times more than it would cost at the present time.
If the federal government has no intention of assisting Toronto in preserving its harbour, I would like the minister to say that now. If they do intend to help Toronto preserve the harbour I would like to know what steps they intend to take. I would like to know how we stand. Does the dominion government intend to help or not:

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would like to know the answer the hon. gentleman received from the province of Ontario.
As I understand it, harbours such as this are a federal responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I told you that high water helps us.
There is deterioration of the harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My officials tell me there is no deterioration of the harbour.

I do not intend to advise the Liberal government how to select a leader for the province of Ontario; if they continue as they have in the past it will be very satisfactory, in my opinion. However, I would like to mention to the minister the drydock contemplated for Collingwood.
This is a coldblooded business proposition, because I believe it is most essential to the shipping facilities on the great lakes. It is the logical location for it, and considerable progress has been made on the project. Owing to the fact that nowadays they are building large tankers and large iron ore carriers it has become more essential than ever that a big drydock capable of handling this type of boat be constructed at Collingwood. Can the minister inform me how rapidly that work might be expected to proceed?
Recently, within the last few months, one of the newer tankers was damaged by fire at Sarnia, and I believe the repairs alone amount to approximately $1J million. They found it necessary to take that boat to the United States for repairs because we have no drydock on the great lakes capable of handling the large tonnage boats that are now being constructed.
I am sure the minister would be glad to give me information on when the work may be started on the new drydock at Collingwood which is so essential to all great lakes shipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand there is a company called the Collingwood Drydock Company that wishes to undertake these works. They are associated with Canada Steamship Lines and they are actually negotiating with the officials of my department to see whether they can come under the Dry Docks Subsidies Act. They are preparing plans, and if they meet the conditions set out in the Dry Docks Subsidies Act they will benefit from the act and get a contribution or a grant spread over so many years. They have hot finalized their plans or the negotiations for this grant.
Thank you very much.

Referring to the point raised by the hon. member for Broadview, my recollection is that when this subject was up in March the minister did say he was getting a report on the situation

from one of his engineers. Am I right in that? And if I am right, has that report been received? Because, as the member for Broadview said, it seems to me it is very desirable that we should know whether any responsibility is assumed here. Somebody certainly should be assuming responsibility, and if the minister's engineer has reported then can we not know; and if he has not, should we not know what is going on?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right; and the engineer reports that it is not our responsibility, that the harbour did not suffer any damages. I just explained before the hon. gentleman came in that for flood situations, high water and damage by storms we have no jurisdiction or responsibility unless the damage is to our own works. As the high water in the harbour of Toronto does not stop the traffic or harm the harbour we have no responsibility for the damage on the island. As I explained, if we were to cover all damage occasioned by storms and floods I would be the first to try to benefit from that responsibility because in my own district, two miles from here, every spring you will see the most terrible flood conditions.
But there is no harbour there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no harbour but people are living right alongside that river.
We are talking about a harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If you are speaking on humanitarian grounds, and as you said a moment ago you were speaking for the people on the island-

As I explained to the minister I am not speaking on humanitarian grounds, because I realize that is not a federal responsibility. I am speaking because I believe this is a harbour which is a federal responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is your opinion, that it is our responsibility. Not being my deputy minister nor my adviser, do you think I should take your opinion on this or take the opinion of those who have spent their lives on these works? Perhaps I am all wrong; perhaps I should tell my officers: Don't tell me these stories; the member for Broadview knows best.

We are beginning to get
somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Up to now I am not
convinced I would be right in doing that.

I am most amazed that the minister took the trouble to send his engineer to investigate the matter if all along it was not a federal responsibility. It seemed to me
55704-235J
Supply-Public Works
that by sending his engineer, the minister agreed that it was a federal responsibility, but I take it that the federal government refuses to do anything in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You will not make me say what I do not want to say. The gentleman asks: why did you send your engineer? What would you have said if I had not sent an engineer to look at the damage?
I would expect you to have said that it was not a federal responsibility and that there was no reason for sending an engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have told you twice
what the report was.
The report of your engineer is different from the report by the city of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am neither the mayor nor a councillor of the city of Toronto. I happen to be the minister of the federal public works department. I have listened to the praise given by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and if you and he agree that we have the best of officials and do the best of jobs, then we will make some progress with these estimates.

I should like to ask a question, but unfortunately I lost my voice down on the Saguenay. Well, I enjoyed the Quebec hospitality down there. I think the minister can hear me. Tonight I am not speaking just about the Fraser valley. One of the Quebec members had a resolution on the order paper concerning river bank erosion on the St. Lawrence. In my own district river bank erosion is the most important thing facing us. I am not talking about harbours now. In the old days the municipality or local authority could care for this, but surely the minister realizes the problem has gone far beyond the ability of the local authority to cope with. He must realize that from his experience in his own district across the river. I thought the minister said, and I should like to be corrected on it, that the request must come from the provincial authority if assistance is required in connection with river bank erosion?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Our department
undertakes certain works when they affect our own federal works or if the damage is caused by our own work or by navigation. That is a clear principle. People suffer from floods or high water or storms, and we believe it is the responsibility of the municipality to cope with the situation. They generally address themselves to the parent who created the municipality, and that is the provincial government. If it is a disaster

Supply-Public Works
of national character and of such importance that the province just cannot cope with it, then the province asks the federal government for help. That is what happened in the Fraser valley flood, in the Winnipeg flood and the Rimouski and Cabano fires. I do not know of any other incidents. We have no direct relationship with the municipalities. They are not our creatures at all. When they have complaints to make they address themselves to the provincial government.

I am afraid the minister did not quite understand me. I am not complaining about the generous treatment we received in so far as the floods were concerned, from both the federal and provincial governments. Unlike the member for Broadview, I am not trying to promote anybody at all. Unfortunately we have no government in British Columbia, so I am promoting nobody out there. However, the Canadian National Railways is one of the most valuable assets of the people of Canada. Am I to understand that in this modern day and age the local municipality-I am not talking about floods or diking now but the natural erosion which occurs every year.- is expected to pay the cost of preventing future river bank erosion such as that which occurred within the last ten months within one hundred yards of the great Canadian National right of way? Is the municipality expected to protect the farmers of the Fraser valley, to protect the Canadian National Railways as well as the investment of the Minister of National Defence of over a million and a half dollars in this area? Am I *to understand that is the responsibility of the local municipality, with a revenue of perhaps $60,000 a year?
From a selfish point of view, I shall tell you the first thing I would have done if I had been Minister of Public Works and the member for that little district across the river, a very enjoyable district. I would have built a dam around that new $2,500,000 building we have been putting up over there, and which has been flooded. I cannot understand why, in this day and age, the Minister of Public Works should tell me it is the responsibility of the local authorities to protect the Canadian National Railways and the investment of the Department of National Defence in a secret naval station. I could tell you what it is. The hon. member for Vancouver South can talk about canoes, but the interceptor station for the whole Pacific coast, in case of a Russian invasion, was endangered within the last ten months by the falling away of a bank. Am I to believe it is the responsibility of a little municipality with a revenue of $50,000 or $60,000 a year
[Mr. Fournier (Hull).l
to protect the Canadian National Railways? One hundred feet of erosion would tie up the whole Pacific coast. It does not make sense to me. I have asked the minister a direct question. Is it the responsibility of the provincial government to make application? Obviously the municipalities cannot apply to the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have stated the general principle, Mr. Chairman, and that policy was announced in the house by the Prime Minister himself. In answer to the hon. member I may say that the Department of Public Works was not set up to protect national defence or the Canadian National Railways. They have their budgets, and they have their obligations. They should protect themselves, and I think they do. Why ask the public works department to do everything that can be done in the country, when it is only one of the departments of government acting under a special statute setting out its jurisdiction? I could be the protector of orphans, the Canadian National Railways and all these works, but they do not come under my department.
I think the member for Vancouver-Quadra was right-
Do not drag me into this fight.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -when he said I was too soft, and that members asked me for all kinds of things. They do not come under my department. To be polite, I am ready to help. If you want me to see someone from the Canadian National to ascertain if they will protect their own property, I can do that. But do not ask the Department of Public Works to take a responsibility which does not come under the department at all.

Before making my few
remarks I should like to make a suggestion to the minister once again. I made one last year, in fact I have made several of them. Whenever the Department of Public Works has men whom they are proud to bring on the floor of the house, I think those men should be introduced to the house. We permit them to come in here to assist the minister, and every time he has new assistants he should introduce them to the house. I know some people near me have asked who these gentlemen are. I happen to know one of them fairly well, perhaps better than he wants to know me. Apart from that, I believe this should be done for the benefit of members who might not have had the opportunity to know these gentlemen.
I want to say that I was rather amazed when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that he was greatly concerned over the public works department. I wonder how

many headaches he would have had if he had had as much to do with the public works department as I have in the last five years, in requesting the construction of a building in Charlottetown known as a post office. Imagine the headaches the member for Van-couver-Quadra would have had if he had had to follow that scheme as I have tried to follow it. Still, I am getting good promises.
I believe those promises will be fulfilled. The minister has been praised tonight as the builder for all the departments, or as the public works man for all the departments. In our case I am afraid he is not even a demol-isher of property, because he and his department have bought a new site for a building they have promised to erect there. They have bought a great deal of property. I understand they have paid for nearly all of it; perhaps they have paid for it all. Now they have become land owners, or property owners, and are renting the property. I suppose they are making quite a good revenue out of it. I know that some of the tenants are paying fairly high rents. The department have a man down there collecting the rents. They are really in the rental business down there.
There is an election coming on next year or probably the year after. What I have been urging them to do is demolish these old buildings and have the site all ready for the new federal building they are going to build there. Time after time we have men down there approaching members and asking them for work. The work they could be doing right now would be demolishing these buildings. The department could get that work done now for a good deal less than it will cost later on when they start to build in a rush. Moreover, by doing it now it would give employment to men who need it today.
So much for the post office. I have been told that we are going to get it. I believe the minister will make good on that promise, because he must make good fairly soon. I know it is going to arrive just in the nick of time, just before the next election.
There was another matter that was mentioned here tonight. I am not going to speak on it now but I just want to say to the Minister of Public Works and to the aides he has with him that I am going to speak on harbour improvements at the appropriate time and also on the building of a marine railway slip, which is another matter to which I have directed attention time and again. There is no disputing that it is a matter that is under this department, because it is for the benefit of the harbour. However, there is an item for that project, and I shall speak on it later. I just want to remind the minister that we still have his promise about
Supply-Public Works
the post office. I feel certain that he will build it. When he will do it is something which it will be up to him to tell us, probably tonight.

There are three items of a general nature that I should like to speak about at this time. One is in connection with the wharf at Portugal Cove. That is a matter which has been raised on several occasions, and on each occasion the minister has said he has no responsibility. I understand that lately there have been conferences between representatives of the provincial government and the federal Department of Public Works on this subject. Portugal Cove is a vital link between the city of St. John's and Bell island. Bell island is the site of the iron ore mines from which between 2 and 3 million tons of iron ore are shipped to the United Kingdom, Germany and Sydney annually. It is an extremely prosperous community. Portugal Cove on the mainland is the place where people have to take a boat and where goods have to be put on board ship to be brought to Bell island.
It seems to me the Department of Public Works should take responsibility for that wharf. There is a tremendous amount of traffic going over it. The great earning power of Bell island is a source of revenue that comes to the federal government through customs and excise duties, sales tax and income tax. There is a big trade between St. John's and Bell island. I should think all of this would be sufficient justification for the minister to say "We will go ahead and we will fix that wharf" and not only fix it but make a decent harbour there. When the princess was there last year, those who have seen the picture "Royal Journey" will remember how rough it was when they were taking the tug to board the liner to take them across the ocean. It is a dangerous harbour in rough weather. There is a big rock right out in front of the wharf. Notwithstanding all the revenue that is pouring into the federal government from Bell island they have not spent any money in connection with it up to the present time. I urge the Minister of Public Works to reconsider his attitude in that respect.
The second matter about which I wish to speak is another hardy annual that has been brought up for consideration each year. I refer to the public building for St. John's. The minister and his officials have been looking around for three years for a site for a public building for St. John's and each year there has been a vote or a revote for that purpose. When the minister is good enough to reply, I should like to know what progress he has made with regard to selecting a site for the public building at St. John's. It

Supply-Public Works
is certainly necessary there. The various departmental offices are all over the place. If he carries out the policy he has adopted elsewhere, he will have a public building erected.
The third point I wish to bring to his attention is in connection with the dredging of the smaller harbours in Newfoundland. Dredging has been going on to a considerable extent in the constituency represented by the Secretary of State, particularly at Bonavista where hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent not only on dredging but on other matters as well. The same thing applies with respect to Grand Bank and Fortune. At these three large settlements dredging has been done. But none has been done in the smaller places, where the fishermen are practically obliged to pole their way in at high water only, such as Renews of which I have spoken half a dozen times here when the estimates have been before the committee. Can the minister not say that something is going to be done for Renews this year? The vote is provided. So will he see that the work is done? It is still a question whether it is going to be done or not, because a dredge may not be sent there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has mentioned three subjects. The first was Portugal Cove. Our difficulties started there because it would be a wharf for the ferry crossing over to the island. This department does not build wharves for ferries, but it builds wharves for the general public use. I am told that my officials down there are negotiating with the province in order to see whether we can come to an understanding with regard to putting up the real facilities that are necessary. If we come to an agreement and have a joint project down there, I think we would go right ahead with it. We have not yet reached that agreement.
As to sites, may I say that I have heard a great deal about a site for that public building at St. John's. I am having trouble in getting a meeting of minds with regard to a site. Personally I favour the Paddock site on government property, which has been recommended to me even by a delegation sent down to St. John's some years ago, on which was Mr. Norman Robertson, clerk of the privy council. I personally spoke with the premier of Newfoundland and he was all ready to sell us that site; but to date, though I have written to the premier to ask what price he wants for it, I have not received an answer. I could hardly conclude that deal without having an answer from the premier of Newfoundland. With my usual 
patience, I am awaiting an answer from the premier with regard to the price he wants for that site.
As to dredging, may I say that we had a new dredge built for the use of the island and for doing dredging in these smaller harbours; but there was a great deal to be done in Newfoundland when it came into union. We have done a considerable amount of work on that island and in the harbours since Newfoundland joined with us. But we cannot do the whole works in one, two or three years. There are 6,000 miles of coast line around that island, and people are living along that coast line. A great many of them are fishermen who expect facilities such as wharves, breakwaters, harbours and dredging. Each year we do a certain amount of that work.
We are still young enough, both the hon. member who put the question and I, that we will see the day when all those harbours will be perfect, and probably the population will be up.

I should like to reply to the first point raised by the minister in connection with this wharf. He speaks of it as a ferry wharf, and because it has so much traffic it is not a place in which the Minister of Public Works considers he should take any interest. Yet he knows that he is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on other wharves where the traffic will not be one per cent of what it is at Portugal Cove. That is not only in Newfoundland, but in other parts of the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Name me one place.
I will name two of them, where the total population is not 300, and where you are spending half a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where is that?

At Chance Harbour and at Lorneville in New Brunswick. He is spending $280,000 in one place and $200,000 in the other. I took the trouble to look up the population of those places. I could not find it myself. I searched in the library, and they did not have the population. The dominion bureau of statistics spent a week trying to find out what the population was.
But there are 10,000 people living on Bell island, and they are doing a tremendous trade as I said before. Yet the minister says this is a ferry wharf. What is the wharf at Digby? Is that not a ferry wharf? Why are you spending money on the wharf at Digby? There is not half as much trade over the wharf at Digby as there is at Portugal Cove.

The minister dealt with several of the matters I mentioned briefly a moment ago, but he did not deal with the evidence given recently by his deputy minister before the public accounts committee concerning the matter of charging the different departments rent for the space occupied by them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That question has been discussed many times in the last ten years. To date the government policy has been to follow the statute which places all public buildings under the control of the Department of Public Works. We meet the


requests of the different departments for their needs.
To establish another branch of the department in which we would charge each department for rental would require an extension of activities. Perhaps it would be a good thing, so far as the other departments are concerned, if they could come to the House of Commons and ask for rent when they present their estimates, but we would have to have some organization to control that. It would simply be a matter of taking money from one pocket and putting it into another. Thus far, and since confederation, the Department of Public Works has provided space for the offices and facilities of other departments. This involves a question of policy which, up to now, has not been changed.

If the minister will read the evidence tendered by his deputy minister before the committee on public accounts a week or so ago he will find in it a very strong condemnation of the present policy, and a strong advocacy of a change in that policy with a view to accomplishing two results: first, truer accounting among different departments of government as to their cost to the public treasury and, second, providing some check upon the demands of departments either for new space or for the retention of space beyond their requirements.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My deputy tells me that he never interferes with government policy. He advises me as to what he thinks best, but policy is decided by the government. As a respectful civil servant he has not tried to dictate policy to the government; at least he has not done so during the ten years he has been with me.
However, there is some good in what he said before that committee, as to the matter of accounting, knowing exactly about expenditures, and how these departments are run. But until the government changes its policy the Department of Public Works must conform to the statute and administer the act the way it is now written.
